House(l) bars using fees received under the section to fund the Legal Orientation Program OR any successor program; it is a restriction on these receipts, not proof the program ended or all other funding was prohibited. House 10012 replaces SNAP2015(f) with its exact version of individual immigration-status conditions. The replacement is a NECESSARY individual-status condition for a member of an OTHERWISE ELIGIBLE household, not a sufficient promise of SNAP entitlement. US RESIDENCE is common to EACH of the four alternatives, AND the individual must meet at least one listed category: (A) a citizen OR NATIONAL of the UNITED STATES; (B) the defined lawful permanent-resident immigrant, retaining the express exclusion of ordinary temporary visitors/tourists/diplomats/students with no intention of abandoning foreign residence; (C) the version's own status category described below; OR (D) an individual lawfully residing in the US IN ACCORDANCE WITH a Compact of Free Association referred to in PRWORA402(b)(2)(G). Complete1101(a)(15)/(20)/(22) defines immigrant/nonimmigrant classes, unchanged lawful permanent residence and US national, without treating every lawful temporary stay or every foreign national as a listed status. Complete1612(b)(2)(G) identifies the US Compacts with the Federated States of Micronesia, Marshall Islands and Palau; nationality alone is not substituted for the proposal's lawful-residence-under-Compact condition. The complete pre-vote2015(f) already requires residence and lists citizen/LPR, the specified1259 deemed-permanent-residence category, conditional entry under1157/1158, the described1182(d)(5) parole and withholding under1231(b)(3). The amendment replaces that subsection's list: its old conditional-entry/general-parole/withholding categories are no longer separate entries, whereas defined permanent residence remains. The new text expressly says citizen OR USnational and supplies its own(C)/(D); it is not described as the first possible benefit for USnationals or COFA residents. Complete pre-vote1611/1612/1613/1641 separately retain qualified-alien definitions, program-specific restrictions/exceptions, the qualified-status five-year framework with its exceptions, and the2024COFA provisions. Qualification alone was not a complete entitlement, nor does the selected replacement directly amend every one of those separate laws. No blanket claim that every refugee, asylee, parolee or other national loses or gains benefits is made; another independently held listed status, other applicable rules and actual eligibility determination remain distinct. The replacement RETAINS consideration of the INELIGIBLE INDIVIDUAL'S income (less a pro-rata share AT STATE OPTION) AND financial resources when determining the eligibility and allotment value of that individual's household. The State-option modifier concerns the income pro-rata subtraction, not exclusion of all financial resources or automatic termination of all household members. The prior statutory paragraph already has this calculation language; it is not a new proof of spending, a specific household's benefit amount or a benefit award. Whole-package votes do not establish component preferences. House(C) requires Cuban citizenship/nationality AND ALL four own predicates: beneficiary of an APPROVED203(a) petition; meeting ALL immigrant-visa eligibility requirements while a visa is NOT IMMEDIATELY AVAILABLE; NOT OTHERWISE INADMISSIBLE under212(a); AND PHYSICAL PRESENCE IN THE US pursuant to parole furthering the specified US commitment to annual legal Cuban migration in the1994/1995joint migration instruments. Complete pre-vote203(a) family-preference rules and the full proposal clause are bound. This is not every Cuban national, a pending petition, any parole, or an actual grant of a visa. House(C) here does NOT require living in Cuba and does not borrow the distinct House70004 parole-FEE exception's living-in-Cuba predicate. Senate's broader defined Cuban/Haitian-entrant phrase is not imported into this House list. House 44110 changes Medicaid and CHIP verification-period assistance and federal payment beginning October 1, 2026. It adds a State option under 1902(a)(46)(C) to make assistance available during the specified reasonable opportunities for citizenship/nationality or satisfactory immigration-status evidence, and during the separate Social Security inconsistency process's 90-day period. It removes the existing obligation to provide assistance during the specified documentary reasonable-opportunity periods when the State has not elected that option; the 1137(d)(4)(A)(ii)/(B)(ii) no-delay/denial/reduction/termination protection is made conditional on that election for MEDICAID, without applying that new Medicaid qualifier to every other program listed in 1137(b). The opportunity to submit evidence and the program's remaining verification processes are not themselves eliminated. New 1903(i)(22)(B) bars federal payment for amounts expended on assistance furnished under that State election during EACH specified citizenship/nationality reasonable-opportunity period, the 90-day period, or the immigration-status reasonable-opportunity period UNLESS the applicable citizenship/nationality or satisfactory immigration status is VERIFIED BY THE END OF THAT PERIOD. State election alone does not assure federal payment, and verification by the end is not described as sufficient to satisfy every other payment condition. The restriction concerns payment to the State for those expenditures, not a factual determination that missing or inconsistent proof establishes unlawful immigration status or permanent ineligibility. CHIP adds (i)(22) to its incorporated payment restrictions and applies the new State option in the same manner as Medicaid. The complete existing 1902(ee) process distinguishes the first reasonable effort to identify and address clerical/name/number/declaration inconsistencies, with assistance continued WHILE MAKING THAT EFFORT, from the subsequent unresolved-inconsistency process. House section 44110 does NOT strike that first continued-assistance clause. The subsequent 90 days run from the date the INDIVIDUAL RECEIVES the notice, not when the State sends it; that period offers documentary evidence OR resolution with Social Security, with continued assistance conditional on State election. The existing text specifies disenrollment within 30 days AFTER THE END of those 90 days using its printed no-documentary-evidence OR unresolved-inconsistency predicate; the amendment adds denial of eligibility AS APPLICABLE. That unamended printed OR is retained rather than silently replaced with AND or treated as a new resolved legal decision on every combined evidentiary path. Existing appeal rights remain. Other reasonable-opportunity periods are not all converted into a fixed 90-day period. Complete 1903(x) retains its own evidence definitions and exceptions for the specified Medicare-enrolled/entitled, disability-benefit/SSI, foster/adoption, newborn and previously documented categories; this is not a new documentary demand on every citizen. Its (x)(5) preserves the stated first-year deemed-eligibility boundary for a US-born child whose alien mother's delivery is available as emergency treatment. Complete 1137(f) excludes the named emergency-treatment cases from (a)(1) and (d); the selected House clause does not amend 1903(v) emergency-payment predicates. No universal immediate cutoff, eliminated appeal, actual State election, individual award or proven savings is inferred. House section 44111 proposes an immigration-linked change to the EXPANSION matching percentage and its related early-expansion formula, not to every Medicaid matching rate. Its quoted amendment to SSA section 1905(y)(1)(E) adds 80 percent, in place of the existing 90-percent expansion percentage for the specified expenditures, ONLY for calendar quarters beginning on or after October 1, 2027 in which the State is a SPECIFIED STATE with respect to that quarter. Complete pre-vote 1905(y) concerns medical assistance for the defined newly eligible 1902(a)(10)(A)(i)(VIII) group in the 50 States/DC, with its own age, December 1, 2009 eligibility and full-benefit definitions. Complete (z)(2) concerns its distinct early-expansion-State/nonpregnant-childless-adult cohort and transition formula; the proposal changes named year references to quarter references so the formula uses the State's quarter percentage. It is not a ten-point reduction of all State medical spending, a universal flat 80-percent Medicaid rate or an actual identified State's funding outcome. The proposed SPECIFIED STATE definition has two alternative quarter-specific triggers, each applying whether the assistance/coverage is inside or outside the Medicaid plan or waiver/another State program, and REGARDLESS OF FUNDING SOURCE. The financial-assistance alternative requires assistance TO OR ON BEHALF OF an alien who is BOTH not a qualified alien under the proposal's modified definition AND not a lawfully US-residing child or pregnant woman RECEIVING MEDICAL ASSISTANCE UNDER 1903(v)(4), FOR purchasing defined health-insurance coverage FOR an alien who ALSO satisfies BOTH of those exclusions. Both recipient/beneficiary positions retain their own exclusions; lawfully residing child/pregnancy status alone without the printed receipt-of-assistance condition is not substituted for the exemption. The other trigger concerns COMPREHENSIVE HEALTH BENEFITS COVERAGE during the quarter for an alien meeting both exclusions. It does not label every emergency-care expenditure comprehensive coverage or every health expense insurance. Complete PHSA section 2791(a)/(b) defines medical care and health-insurance coverage offered by an issuer under the named policies/service contracts, with its own licensed/regulatory issuer definition. The proposal uses the incorporated alien definition and modifies qualified alien under 1641: it excludes the (b)(4) parole category OTHER THAN the printed qualified-alien-under 402(b)(2) carveout; it shifts the named status-assessment wording from benefit application, receipt or attempted receipt to provision of the specified coverage or financial assistance; and it substitutes the State's opinion in the named battered-individual clauses for the agency-providing-benefits opinion. Complete 1641 and 1612 authorities are bound. This is not an assertion that every parolee is excluded, that every lawful immigrant is a qualified alien, or that any actual State has made the required battered-individual or coverage determination. The governing floor and EH witness retain the literal parenthetical 42 U.S.C. 1395d after SSA section 1905, although the bound Code identifies 1395d as SSA 1812 Medicare benefits and 1396d as SSA 1905 Medicaid definitions/FMAP. The proposed definition's quoted 1905(y)(C) references are shortened relative to the new (y)(2)(C) placement. Neither printed reference is silently repaired or substituted; their application is separately reserved for independent source-grounded review. The complete H.Res. 492 corrections do not correct section 44111. The candidate describes the quoted rate, quarter and defined-State mechanisms with that qualification; it does not claim a resolved legal crosswalk or actual funding loss. The printed wavier typo also remains in the unchanged source, without a new semantic claim. House section 112103 proposes a new Medicare immigration-status restriction with its own Cuban category and existing-enrollee transition. The new section 1899C makes a listed immigration/citizenship category NECESSARY for entitlement to or enrollment in Title XVIII benefits, subject to its own existing-enrollee transition; the list is not sufficient entitlement, an award or proof that a person satisfies all other Medicare requirements. It lists US citizen OR US national, lawful permanent residence under the INA, the version's own category(3), OR lawful US residence in accordance with a referenced Compact of Free Association. Unlike the new SNAP/Medicaid lists, 1899C(a) does not print a NEW COMMON RESIDENCE modifier across every alternative; the COFA alternative keeps its own lawful-residence predicate and other existing Medicare residence rules retain their own scopes. Complete material pre-vote 226/226A/1836 and 1818(a)/1818A(a) are bound. They distinguish hospital entitlement through the named age/insured-benefit, disability/railroad/government-employment or renal-disease pathways from separate Part B or premium Part A enrollment paths. In 1836(a), existing Part A entitlement is an ALTERNATIVE to the age 65/US-resident branch, whose citizen OR LPR alternatives have a five-year continuous-residence condition on the LPR branch. Complete 1818(a) has its own age 65, Part B enrollment, US residence, citizen OR LPR-with-five-years and no-other-Part-A-entitlement conjunction. The five-year modifier is not applied to every citizen, every enrollee or every entitlement path. The limited 1836(b) post-renal immunosuppressive-drug enrollment and own other-coverage exclusions remain distinct from full benefits. Complete 1818A(a) preserves its own disabled/earnings-related premium eligibility, not a generic disability guarantee. Neither age alone nor listed status alone is described as sufficient; the selected proposal does not directly rewrite each underlying benefit rule or establish an exhaustive pre-vote eligibility universe. The transition applies specifically to individuals ENTITLED TO OR ENROLLED FOR Title XVIII benefits AS OF ENACTMENT. The Commissioner must review that cohort to identify people not described in ANY of the four listed alternatives, and notify EACH identified person of termination at the enactment-relative date, as soon as practicable AFTER IDENTIFICATION and in a manner designed to ensure comprehension. The termination date is not measured from receipt or sending of the notice; the review deadline is not the termination date. No identical grace period is promised to every later applicant, perpetual grandfathering, actual completed review, actual termination or observed administrative outcome is inferred. Enactment-relative dates are not converted into dates based on this vote or the later enacted law. House category(3) requires Cuban citizenship/nationality AND ALL four own conditions: an APPROVED 203(a) petition; meeting ALL immigrant-visa eligibility requirements while a visa is NOT IMMEDIATELY AVAILABLE; NOT OTHERWISE INADMISSIBLE under 212(a); AND PHYSICAL US PRESENCE pursuant to parole furthering the specified 1994/1995 annual-legal-migration commitment. It is not every Cuban national, pending petition or any parole, and contains no living-in-Cuba condition borrowed from the separate parole-fee exception. The complete proposed category and incorporated 203(a) baseline are bound. Its transition makes the restriction apply to the existing-enrollee cohort ONE YEAR AFTER ENACTMENT, with the review completed NOT LATER THAN SIX MONTHS AFTER ENACTMENT and the comprehensible notice tied to that one-year termination date. No Senate defined-entrant substitution, 18-month grace or one-year review deadline is imported. House sections 112101/112102 propose their own ACA alien-status and special-income-rule changes. The selected ACA status provision adds lawfully present aliens who are NOT eligible aliens to 36B(e)(1), whose named condition concerns one or more individuals for whom the taxpayer is allowed a section 151 deduction (including taxpayer or spouse), and whose complete existing mechanism reduces the portion of counted premiums attributable to the affected INDIVIDUAL and adjusts family-size/household-income calculations using the specified fraction or comparable method. It is not automatic loss of every otherwise eligible household member's credit or a blanket ban on insurance enrollment. Existing 36B(e)(2) whole-period citizenship/nationality/lawful-presence wording is retained as subparagraph(A); the new eligible-alien provision concerns an individual who IS AN ALIEN AND LAWFULLY PRESENT and who IS, AND IS REASONABLY EXPECTED TO BE FOR THE ENTIRE CREDIT-ENROLLMENT PERIOD, within its own listed LPR, version-specific Cuban-related, OR COFA-lawful-residence category. Both current status and the reasonable whole-period expectation remain, common to the listed alternatives; a single day of status, nationality alone or any lawful temporary stay is not substituted. Citizens/US nationals are not required to fit the new alien-only list. Separate applicable-taxpayer, income, coverage-month, plan/enrollment and other credit requirements remain; status alone is not sufficient. The companion provision deletes 36B(c)(1)(B), whose complete pre-vote special rule requires ALL of household income NOT GREATER THAN 100 percent of the family poverty line, LAWFUL PRESENCE as an alien, AND Medicaid ineligibility BY REASON OF THAT ALIEN STATUS, then treats that taxpayer as applicable with income equal to 100 percent for credit purposes. It is not every Medicaid-ineligible person, any low income or a finding that the person lacks lawful presence. Deletion removes that special treatment for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025; it does not alone prove that EVERY person at EXACTLY 100 percent loses the credit, because ordinary (c)(1)(A) begins at 100 percent subject to its other rules. The temporary 2021-2025 upper-income rule and complete coverage predicates are separately bound, without extending it into future years or quantifying an actual credit. The status provision's non-conforming amendments apply to TAXABLE YEARS BEGINNING AFTER DECEMBER 31, 2026; its conforming amendments apply to PLAN YEARS BEGINNING ON OR AFTER JANUARY 1, 2027. Those tax/plan-year bases remain distinct from the earlier special-rule repeal; neither vote date nor later enacted implementation dates are substituted. Both status versions replace the lawful-alien phrase in 5000A(d)(3) with the eligible-alien reference; they do NOT change the bound penalty calculation's existing zero-dollar/zero-percent components. No revived monetary mandate penalty or actual tax/benefit determination is inferred. House 36B(e)(2)(B) prints IF AND ONLY IF for eligible-alien treatment. Its Cuban alternative requires Cuban nationality AND ALL approved 203(a)-petition, all-visa-eligibility-but-no-immediate-visa, no-other-inadmissibility and physical-US-presence-under-the-specified 1994/1995-parole-commitment predicates; it has no living-in-Cuba condition from the different parole-fee exception. The common lawful-presence/current-and-whole-period-expectation conditions apply to that alternative too. The Senate's granted entrant definition is not imported. House 112101 conforms 1411 verification for premium credits AND reduced cost-sharing, 1412 federal-payment restriction, 1402(e) individual cost-sharing/family calculations and its own eligible-alien whole-period condition, and 1331(e)(1) basic-health eligible-individual exclusion. The quoted basic-health insertion retains its printed unfinished parenthetical; no governing bytes are repaired. These are direct House amendments to their named programs, not the same scope as the Senate's selected conforming text. Complete underlying program predicates remain: no automatic award for a listed status or whole-household cost-sharing loss is asserted. House 112102 also renumbers the remaining 36B(c)(1) subparagraphs, adjusts its named 2021 cross-reference, removes the lawfully-present/Medicaid-alien-status special branch from basic-health 1331(e)(1)(B), and deletes 1402(b)'s second sentence importing the special credit rule. The cost-sharing and basic-health provisions have their own eligibility/thresholds; their removal is not reduced to a universal tax-credit outcome. House section 112201 proposes its own Exchange verification and filing-compliance conditions. The selected Exchange verification provision adds credit coverage-month conditions for an INDIVIDUAL enrolled in a qualified health plan through an Exchange. A month beginning BEFORE the specified verification is excluded unless the own past-month verification clause is met; this is not an assertion that all earlier months are permanently lost. Applicable information must be PROVIDED OR VERIFIED BY THE APPLICANT, with affirmation of at least the listed information TO THE EXTENT RELEVANT to the specified eligibility. Both versions expressly say failure of this paragraph ALONE does NOT make an individual ineligible to enroll through the Exchange for that month. Credit coverage-month, advance payment, reduced cost-sharing and enrollment are distinct; no insurance-enrollment ban, actual credit award/loss or guaranteed verification date is inferred. Both versions separately exclude a plan from the tax provision's qualified-health-plan definition UNLESS the Exchange PROVIDES a pre-enrollment verification PROCESS through which ANY APPLICANT MAY, BEGINNING NOT LATER THAN AUGUST 1, verify the version-specific information/eligibility for plans in the SUBSEQUENT PLAN YEAR. This is an Exchange process availability deadline, not a requirement that each applicant must submit or complete verification by August 1, a universal enrollment period or a promise of coverage. Amendments in these selected sections apply to TAXABLE YEARS BEGINNING AFTER DECEMBER 31, 2027; the incorporated Senate rule's post-2025 scope is not substituted as the statute's effective date. House coverage-month verification requires ALL eligibility to enroll, for ANY advance premium credit payment, AND for ANY reduced cost-sharing. Its information list separately names income, ANY immigration status, any coverage status/eligibility, residence, family size and authorized other necessary information. Past-month verification prints IF AND ONLY IF and retains all three eligibility branches FOR THAT MONTH. The pre-enrollment process covers enrollment, advance credit AND reduced cost-sharing, rather than the Senate's household-income/enrollment scope. The House filing-compliance clause names the full 45 CFR 155.305(f)(4) AS PUBLISHED MARCH 19, 2025 (90 FR 12942). That publication is a PROPOSED RULE, not the June final rule or a later/current CFR. Its complete printed amendment revises the one-year filing/reconciliation condition and notice alternatives and removes/reserves(ii). The condition requires HHS notification through the specified process that advance payments were made for the tax filer OR either spouse in the married-couple case for the YEAR WHOSE TAX DATA WOULD BE USED for income/family verification, and that the filer or spouse failed to file the required return and reconcile the advances. It is not a filing test for every person regardless of prior advance payments or the named notification/data conditions. The proposed notice alternatives retain tax-information protection: direct notification to the filer of failure and need to file/reconcile immediately on receipt, OR risk/education notification to the filer or enrollee without directly stating the IRS failure indication. No later adopted regulation, determination that the proposal independently became law, automatic household enrollment termination or guaranteed notice-to-loss interval is substituted. The related House section 44201(b)(1) income-verification amendment applies to PLAN YEARS BEGINNING ON OR AFTER JANUARY 1, 2026. If requested Treasury household-income data is NOT RETURNED, income may not be verified SOLELY by that individual's attestation, and the Exchange must take existing 1411(e)(4)(A) actions; it is not an automatic coverage/credit denial. Its specified-income-discrepancy branch requires ALL of an attested projected annual household income qualifying under 36B(c)(1)(A), Treasury OR RELIABLE third-party data indicating income below that applicable-taxpayer floor, an excess over the data by an Exchange-established AND Secretary-approved reasonable threshold of NOT LESS THAN 10 PERCENT (which may ALSO be a dollar amount), AND no Exchange assessment/determination from those data that household income meets the applicable Medicaid OR CHIP income standard. Clause (iii) excludes from THIS DISCREPANCY SUBPARAGRAPH an applicant who is LAWFULLY PRESENT AS AN ALIEN AND Medicaid-ineligible BY REASON OF ALIEN STATUS. It does not exempt all immigrants, every Medicaid-ineligible person or the separate missing-Treasury-data branch. The bound existing 1411(e)/(f) process keeps citizenship/lawful-presence inconsistencies in(e)(3) separate from other-information(e)(4): reasonable clerical/contact effort, then notice and opportunity to provide satisfactory documents OR resolve with the verifying person during 90 days starting WHEN NOTICE IS SENT. The Medicaid individual-receipt clock is not imported. Existing provisional application-based determinations except the citizenship/presence branch, unresolved credit/reduction amount notice and appeals remain distinct from an automatic loss or every issue receiving the same opportunity. The annual filing and automatic-extension provisions are addressed separately below. House section 44201(b)(2)/(3) adds separate annual filing and income-opportunity provisions. Its annual advance-credit rule applies to PLAN YEARS BEGINNING ON OR AFTER JANUARY 1, 2026 for an individual whose prior advance premium credit was paid TO THE PLAN ISSUER for the RELEVANT PRIOR TAX YEAR. That year means the tax year whose return data WOULD BE USED for household-income/family-size verification, not automatically the immediately preceding calendar year. An advance eligibility determination may not be made IF THE EXCHANGE DETERMINES FROM TREASURY INFORMATION that the individual has NOT FILED a return AS REQUIRED under sections 6011/6012 OR, AS NECESSARY, has NOT RECONCILED the advance payment under 36B(f). Those return-required, reconciliation-required, prior-payment and determination conditions are retained; it is not a filing duty for every enrollee or a finding of a particular tax debt. The complete underlying reconciliation mechanism distinguishes credit netting and excess-payment tax treatment with its own pre-vote qualifications, without calculating an actual liability. If an affected individual ATTESTS fulfillment of return filing AND, AS NECESSARY, reconciliation for that relevant year, the Secretary MAY make an INITIAL advance eligibility determination AND MAY DELAY FOR A REASONABLE PERIOD, AS THE SECRETARY DETERMINES, a Treasury-based contrary determination. Attestation does not permanently override Treasury information or guarantee approval. IF the Secretary determines noncompliance AND NOTIFIES THE EXCHANGE, the Exchange must comply with 155.305(f)(4)(i) AS IN EFFECT FOR PLAN YEAR 2025. Its direct protected notice to the filer OR indirect risk/education notice to filer/enrollee is bound at the pre-vote annual text, with the January 2025 addition of (ii) separately checked: that intervening amendment does not change (i). The referenced (i) retains its printed second-consecutive-year risk wording; neither the March proposed immediately-upon-receipt wording nor the June final notice is silently substituted for this DIFFERENT statutory reference. Its relationship to the newly stated annual determination remains qualified rather than a guaranteed delay or an invented notice-to-loss period. The separate(b)(3) provision directs removal of 155.315(f)(7) for PLAN YEARS BEGINNING ON OR AFTER JANUARY 1, 2026, so an Exchange providing the named 90-day inconsistency opportunity may NOT AUTOMATICALLY EXTEND IT ON THE BASIS THAT THE APPLICANT MUST PRESENT SATISFACTORY HOUSEHOLD-INCOME DOCUMENTS. The governed pre-vote (f)(7) supplies that automatic 60-day income-document extension. This is not removal of every opportunity or extension, a universal 90-day cutoff, or a citizenship-status finding: bound (f)(3) separately permits extension if demonstrated GOOD-FAITH EFFORT to obtain documentation, and(f)/(g) retain their own clerical, notice-sent clock, conditional interim-assistance, data/determination and special-circumstance rules. The latter case-by-case documentary exception expressly excludes citizenship/immigration-status inconsistencies. May-vote floor successor-regulation wording remains literal; later House corrections do not replace it. The DACA-specific provisions are addressed separately below; other package components remain unfinished. Complete pre-vote section 1402(g) adds a material boundary to the selected ACA cost-sharing comparison: NO cost-sharing reduction is allowed for coverage for ANY MONTH UNLESS that month is a COVERAGE MONTH FOR WHICH A SECTION 36B CREDIT IS ALLOWED TO THE INSURED OR AN APPLICABLE TAXPAYER ON THE INSURED'S BEHALF. This is a necessary credit/month dependency, not a sufficient entitlement, and it does not require every insured to be the tax filer personally. Shared terms take section 36B meanings; eligibility data use the taxable year of the ADVANCE DETERMINATION, not the taxable year for which the credit is allowed. Retaining a cost-sharing sentence or basic-health branch alone therefore does not establish continuing reductions or an award. Individual/family calculations, own program predicates and the direct House/Senate amendment distinctions remain; residual cross-reference/program application stays RESERVED as question 34. No individual credit, reduction or basic-health outcome is adjudicated. House section 112104 proposes a 3.5 PERCENT remittance tax with its own verification exception, new credit and reporting structure. Both selected remittance sections require the SENDER to pay the tax, the PROVIDER to collect it FROM THE SENDER AND remit QUARTERLY as prescribed by the Secretary, and secondary provider liability ONLY TO THE EXTENT the tax is unpaid at transfer AND not collected. These are separate payer, collection and secondary-liability roles, not a tax only on providers or a charge already observed. Both deem the remittance a financing transaction for the specified multiple-party anti-conduit authority; existing 7701(l) permits appropriate regulation/recharacterization, not an automatic finding of evasion or wrongdoing. Transfer amendments apply to TRANSFERS MADE AFTER DECEMBER 31, 2025, not the vote date or a substituted later enacted date. The bound remittance definitions concern an ELECTRONIC, PROVIDER-INITIATED funds transfer requested by a CONSUMER/NATURAL-PERSON SENDER LOCATED IN A DEFINED STATE to an AUTHORIZED DESIGNATED RECIPIENT LOCATED IN A FOREIGN COUNTRY. Consumer/State, electronic and normal-course provider definitions are independently bound, with account-independence and the statutory SMALL-VALUE EXCLUSION retained. This is not every domestic payment, every cross-border business transaction, every family expense or a recipient-citizenship test. Electronic transfer technology and the Senate physical FUNDING instrument are different predicates. No specific transaction, person, provider, regulatory threshold or actual tax outcome is classified. The House exception requires BOTH a QUALIFIED REMITTANCE PROVIDER with a WRITTEN AGREEMENT WITH THE SECRETARY to verify citizen/national status by prescribed procedures AND a sender VERIFIED BY THAT QUALIFIED PROVIDER AS A US CITIZEN OR NATIONAL pursuant to the agreement. It is not an automatic exception for any asserted citizen, every provider or every SSN holder. Citizen and national remain distinct statutory terms. The House defines remittance terms by printing EFTA SECTION 920(g) alongside 15 USC 1693o-1, while the complete pre-vote Code source credit maps 1693o-1 to SECTION 919 and 1693o-2 card text to SECTION 920. That printed House Act/Code reference mismatch stays literal and separately RESERVED; the Senate's 919(g) is not silently substituted. The available definitions are bound as candidate context, not an adjudicated legal crosswalk. The House separately proposes new 36C: its heading names citizens/nationals, while (a) prints IN THE CASE OF ANY INDIVIDUAL and credits aggregate 4475 taxes PAID BY THAT INDIVIDUAL DURING THE TAXABLE YEAR. No credit is allowed unless the return includes the individual's SSN AND, IF MARRIED, the spouse's SSN, with the defined SSA issuance/due-date restrictions; rules SIMILAR to 32(d) apply. The same House 110004 amendment extends 24(h) and replaces (h)(7), preserving the definition's US-citizen OR named lawful/work-authorized alien issuance branch and BEFORE-DUE-DATE condition. A qualifying number is not proof of US citizenship and not every tax identifier qualifies; child-credit claimant provisions are not imported into 36C. Complete SSA assignment and 32(d) joint-return/separated-spouse baselines are bound without automatically converting SIMILAR rules into identical personal determinations. The credit also requires demonstration TO THE SECRETARY'S SATISFACTION that the 4475 tax WAS PAID BY THE TAXPAYER AND concerned a transfer for which the taxpayer supplied the certification/information referred to in 6050BB(a)(2). Heading versus ANY-INDIVIDUAL operative scope, the marriage/SSN cross-reference and the reporting predicate remain separately reserved for application; no universal citizen refund, automatic noncitizen denial/eligibility or actual credit is asserted. New 6050BB separates aggregate qualified-provider exempt-transfer reporting, individual certified-intent reporting with the printed INFORMATION DESCRIBED IN PARAGRAPH (1) reference and named-person/tax-paid/tax-remitted items, and aggregate other-transfer tax reporting. The provider furnishes a statement to EACH NAMED PERSON as prescribed. The awkward introductory information cross-reference is not repaired into another paragraph, and SSN reporting for every transfer is not inferred. Conforming reporting/refund/math-error text remains literal, without determining penalties or actual refunds. The selected transfer provisions start after December 31, 2025; the new credit and its named conforming amendments instead apply to TAXABLE YEARS ENDING AFTER DECEMBER 31, 2025, not taxable years BEGINNING then. That temporal distinction, explicit substantiation and unresolved printed references prevent an automatic net-cost claim. No Senate cash-only limitation, noncash exemption or lack of credit mechanism is imported into the House version. House section 44201(i) adds three distinct ACA lawful-presence provisions for an ALIEN GRANTED DEFERRED ACTION under the DACA process PURSUANT TO THE NAMED JUNE 15, 2012 MEMORANDUM; satisfying historical criteria, filing a request or having work authorization alone is not the printed grant condition. New 1312(f)(4) says IN THIS TITLE the term alien lawfully present does not include that granted-DACA group. The added 1402(e)(2) sentence says FOR PURPOSES OF THIS SECTION that individual shall not be treated as lawfully present. The added 1412(d) sentence says FOR PURPOSES OF THE PREVIOUS SENTENCE, whose own subject is Federal payments, credits and cost-sharing reductions for individuals not lawfully present. These are separate defined scopes, not revocation of every immigration status, deferral, work permit or insurance policy. Subsection (i)(4) prints that amendments MADE BY THIS SECTION apply WITH RESPECT TO PLAN YEARS BEGINNING ON OR AFTER JANUARY 1, 2026; that wording is preserved alongside the other distinct 44201 dates, without a personal termination date or silently narrowing its section referent. Complete pre-vote 1312(f) concerns qualified individuals and INDIVIDUAL-MARKET QUALIFIED PLANS OFFERED THROUGH AN EXCHANGE, with State residence, custody/pending-disposition distinction and current AND reasonably expected ENTIRE ENROLLMENT PERIOD citizenship/nationality/lawful-presence predicates. Complete 1402(b)/(e) retains its silver-plan, income and individual/family allocation boundaries: a named individual is not a finding that an entire mixed-status household loses coverage or reductions. Complete 1402(g) separately makes an allowed 36B credit for the coverage month, to the insured OR taxpayer on behalf, necessary but not sufficient for reductions. Complete 1412 has its own advance determination/issuer-payment mechanics; its pre-vote State-flexibility sentence permits additional State payments, rather than a guaranteed State award or an adjudicated workaround under the proposed amendments. No universal all-insurance ban, individual benefit loss, effective current regulation or litigation outcome is inferred. The original June 15, 2012 Napolitano memorandum is governed as historical identity and full policy context, from the actual official Supreme Court-hosted signed three-page scan and DOJ Appendix E reproduction. Its five criteria and distinct paths remain source-bound: under-sixteen arrival, continuous residence for the printed five-year period AND presence on the memo date, the listed education/service alternatives, the printed criminal/public-safety criterion and not above thirty. Original wording including "for a least five years" and "or otherwise poses a threat" is retained in the witnesses without inserting a missing word or building a personal eligibility classifier. Background check AND CASE-BY-CASE determination and NO ASSURANCE OF RELIEF remain. ICE/CBP encounter discretion and existing USCIS notice-to-appear guidance differ from ICE pending-removal/no-final-order two-year renewable deferral and the separate USCIS non-removal process with AT LEAST 15 and two-year renewable deferral. Original 60-day implementation directions are relative to the MEMO DATE, not new bill deadlines. The final-order USCIS sentence prints REGARDLESS OF THEIR AGE: its relationship to the minimum age and the other age criterion is RESERVED as question 38, without globalizing the minimum age or declaring all age criteria waived. For an ICE/USCIS deferred-action grantee, USCIS accepts APPLICATIONS TO DETERMINE WHETHER THEY QUALIFY for work authorization during deferral, not an automatic work permit. The memo confers NO SUBSTANTIVE RIGHT, IMMIGRATION STATUS OR PATHWAY TO CITIZENSHIP; that disclaimer does not independently determine ACA lawful-presence treatment. Original policy text is not evidence of a current individual grant, current DACA eligibility/legal validity or current ACA application. Its rationale is not adopted as a claim about any person's motives. Selected House section 110004 child-credit identification provisions require the return to include the TAXPAYER'S SSN AND QUALIFYING CHILD'S SSN AND, IF MARRIED, THE SPOUSE'S SSN. Its (C) separately applies rules SIMILAR TO 32(d), whose complete marital rule includes joint-return treatment and its defined separated-spouse exception; similarity is not automatically identical application or a universal denial for every separately filing spouse. The child-credit amendments apply to TAXABLE YEARS BEGINNING AFTER DECEMBER 31, 2024. Full section context extends 24(h). The $2,500 substitution applies to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, and before December 31, 2028. The $2,000 substitution applies to any subsequent taxable year. Its separate credit-amount inflation applies in a taxable year beginning after 2028. Own refundable ceilings and rounding remain; these nominal amounts are not an award to every household. House 110003 has its different after-2025 date for the zero-exemption extension. This is selected child-credit/SSN context, not complete interpretation of religious-association earned-income or every tax-package component. The child-credit comparison is with the complete pre-vote 24(a)-(h), not its separate historical 2021 regime. Before either amendment, 24(h)(7) required the QUALIFYING CHILD'S defined SSN; the new clauses add claimant-side conditions without changing that child prerequisite. An SSN is not alone citizenship proof. Both new definitions permit SSA issuance to either a US citizen or an individual under the named work-authorized-alien branch, including the specified catch-up portion. In either case, the SSN must have been issued before the due date for the return. Any other SSA issuance purpose or an ITIN does not alone satisfy this definition. Complete SSA issuance text distinguishes those branches. Section 24(c) retains an incorporated 152(c) qualifying child AND its own NOT-ATTAINED-17 requirement and its separate citizenship/residence limitation; complete 152 preserves relationship, abode/support, joint-return/refund, competing-claim, adopted/foster, custody/release and missing-child exceptions. Neither a valid SSN nor a citizenship label establishes all credit prerequisites. Own income/phaseout, earned-income/refund, tax/identification/year and other conditions remain; credit/refund figures are not guaranteed payments. Retained 24(h)(4) is separate: (A) provides a $500 other-dependent branch with own (B) noncitizen boundary, and (C) says a qualifying child not allowed credit BY REASON OF PARAGRAPH (7) is treated as a dependent to whom (A) applies. Neither bill strikes that text. Its application to newly added taxpayer/spouse SSN failures is RESERVED as question 39; no automatic fallback award, complete household-credit loss or claim about every dependent is made. Pre-vote 151(d)(5)(B) says reducing the exemption amount to zero is NOT TAKEN INTO ACCOUNT in determining allowed/allowable/entitled deductions for OTHER TITLE PROVISIONS, so zero exemptions alone do not establish no child credit. The exact same-bill 151(d)(5) amendments extend the zero-exemption period while retaining that reference rule; distinct own dates and separately addressed Senate senior provisions are not merged into this child-credit description. Both amend 6213(g)(2)(I) from section 24(e) to SECTION 24 for omission of a correct identification number; this mathematical-or-clerical-error mechanism is not a finding of fraud, corruption, an actual debt or removal of all remedies. Complete 6213(b)(1)/(2) requires notice of the alleged error AND explanation, distinguishes that notice from a deficiency notice/no petition BASED ON THAT NOTICE, permits an abatement request WITHIN 60 DAYS AFTER NOTICE IS SENT, requires abatement UPON RECEIPT of that request, subjects reassessment to deficiency procedures and stays levy/court collection during the abatement period. No actual notice, filing deadline, assessment, successful claim or taxpayer classification is inferred. House section 110103 prints a $4,000 bonus increase in the amount in section 63(f)(1), for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, and before January 1, 2029. The pre-vote aged paragraph has separate branches. Its taxpayer amount requires the taxpayer to have attained 65 before the tax year closes. Its separate spouse amount requires the spouse to have attained 65 before that close and an additional exemption for that spouse to be allowable to the taxpayer under section 151(b). These inherited predicates do not establish an actual bonus or override the new identification, marital or reserved quotation-boundary limits. The distinct blind paragraph is not a grant of this bonus to every blind younger person. The bonus is reduced, but not below zero, by 4 percent of modified adjusted gross income over $75,000, or over $150,000 on a joint return. The return must include the taxpayer's defined SSN and, if married, the spouse's defined SSN. Rules similar to section 32(d) are separately incorporated, with its defined separated-spouse context; similarity is not automatically identical application or a universal separate-return denial. Printed (E) says section 63(c)(4) does not apply to a dollar amount in this new paragraph, rather than removing every existing standard-deduction inflation adjustment. Printed (F) describes an itemizer deduction for the aggregate increase that would be determined under (A), after applying (B), (D) and (E), if the taxpayer had not elected to itemize. Its own window is a taxable year beginning after December 31, 2024, and before January 1, 2029. The hypothetical increase and all named conditions remain; this is not an automatic $4,000 for every itemizer or a resolved override of standard-deduction exclusions. The governing floor closes a quotation after the SSN definition before printed (E)/(F), unlike later EH formatting. Substantive words match under a declared formatting-only comparison, and no H.Res.492 item targets this section. Both original witnesses remain; later EH does not replace the May vote source. Exact quotation-boundary application is reserved as question 40, so printed (E)/(F) are qualified candidate mechanisms, without silent repair or settled individual application. The inherited SSN definition is the same version's amended section 24(h)(7). It permits SSA issuance to either a US citizen or an individual under the named work-authorized-alien branch, including the specified catch-up portion. In either case, the number must have been issued before the due date for the return. An ITIN or any other SSA number does not alone satisfy the definition, and the listed alien branch is not citizenship-only. The child-credit joint-return alternative does not replace the senior deduction's identification condition. Full marital authorities retain their own reference scopes and conditional separated-spouse rules; this description does not determine anyone's marital status. Complete section 63 preserves taxable-income and itemization mechanics and its own standard-deduction exclusions, including a nonresident alien individual. Section 151 retains its own spouse/exemption references and zero-exemption rule for other-provision deduction references. These are source-bound prerequisites, rather than eligibility for every alien, senior or itemizer or an accepted override of an exclusion. A deduction is not a dollar-for-dollar credit, an exemption of all Social Security benefits or a guaranteed refund. Both versions' senior amendments apply to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024. Each version retains its own printed limit for a taxable year beginning before January 1, 2029. Both modified-income definitions add amounts excluded under sections 911, 931 and 933. No personal amount, return, age, marriage, residency or tax outcome is determined. Each adds its own mathematical-error omission reference: House (Z) names its section 63(f)(5)(D), while Senate (W) names its section 151(d)(5)(C). Those labels and provisions are not interchangeable. The inherited notice rules require an alleged error and explanation; the no-petition rule concerns a petition based on that notice. An abatement request may be filed within 60 days after the notice is sent. On receipt of that request the assessment must be abated, any reassessment uses deficiency procedures, and levy/court collection is stayed during the abatement period. No actual debt, fraud or loss of every remedy is inferred. Selected House section 112105 requires the taxpayer's defined SSN on the return for both education credits. If the individual is married, the spouse's defined SSN is also required. If the credit concerns qualified tuition and related expenses of an individual other than the taxpayer or spouse, that other individual's name and defined SSN are also required. The taxpayer-number requirement applies in every listed case; the conditional spouse and other-student requirements do not replace it. House separately replaces section 25A(g)(6) with rules similar to section 32(d), whose complete joint-return and defined separated-spouse context is bound. Similarity is not automatically identical application, and no universal separate-return denial or personal marital determination is made. Both selected education sections replace section 25A(g)(1), whose subsection (a) covers the American Opportunity Tax Credit and Lifetime Learning Credit. Before amendment, the general student name and taxpayer-identification-number rule applied to both credits, while the additional student/taxpayer issuance-date and institution-number rules were AOTC-specific. The new defined-SSN condition applies to both credits. Both inherit their own same-bill amended section 24(h)(7) definition: SSA issuance to either a US citizen or the named work-authorized-alien branch, including its specified catch-up portion. In either case, the number must have been issued before the return due date. Any SSA number or an ITIN does not alone meet that definition; it is not citizenship-only. The old AOTC student deadline says on or before the due date, while the new definition says before. Those exact bounds are preserved. Child-credit claimant alternatives and senior each-person rules do not replace the education section's named roles. Both new institution clauses concern only the American Opportunity Tax Credit: the taxpayer must include the employer identification number of any institution to which the taxpayer paid qualified tuition and related expenses taken into account under section 25A on the tax-year return. That is not a new institution-number requirement for Lifetime Learning or for every institution irrespective of the named payments. Expenses paid by a qualifying dependent retain section 25A(g)(3)'s treatment as paid by the other taxpayer; the dependent cannot independently claim the credit under that paragraph. Full dependent and zero-exemption reference conditions remain, without an individual family determination. Material credit prerequisites remain. AOTC has its per-student, election, four-prior-year, first-four-postsecondary-years, eligible-academic-period, half-time and named felony-drug/prior-claim restrictions. Lifetime Learning has its per-taxpayer expense and job-skills/course context. Own income phaseouts, excluded-income additions, expense definitions and nonacademic/sports exclusions, assistance reductions, prepayments, double-benefit prohibition, payee-statement exception, partial-AOTC-refund/child restriction and recapture authority remain. A defined number is necessary under the new identification clause, rather than proof of all student, expense, credit or refund prerequisites. The AOTC eligible-student reference names HEA 484(a)(1), as in effect when section 25A was enacted, and separately requires at least half the normal full-time course load. It does not name the whole of current 484(a), including its separate citizenship paragraph. The institution definition separately requires the frozen HEA 481 description and eligibility to participate in a title IV program. Code reference notes identify the frozen date as August 5, 1997. Historical 1996 and 1997 witnesses preserve the selected student enrollment/credential provision, its preparatory-course and teacher-credential exceptions, and the complete referenced institution conditions, including their incorporated historical definitions. Selected student and incorporated institution-definition passages match exactly; full HEA 481 operative words match only after two declared split-word comparisons. Original texts remain unchanged. Annual dates alone do not establish personal or institutional eligibility, and neither current student-aid eligibility nor a new House student-aid provision is silently substituted for those frozen tax references. The retained nonresident rule applies if the taxpayer was a nonresident alien for any portion of the tax year. Section 25A applies only if that individual is treated as a resident for chapter 1 by a section 6013(g) or (h) election. The (g) path requires the named nonresident individual at year close to be married to a citizen or resident and both spouses to make the election. Its duration, neither-spouse-resident nonapplication, termination and re-election limits remain. The (h) path requires nonresident status at year beginning, resident status at year close, marriage at year close to a citizen or resident, and both individuals' prescribed election; its own one-election limit remains. Tax-resident treatment for the specified chapters does not grant immigration status, work authorization, citizenship or a credit automatically. This is not a categorical denial to every noncitizen. Both sections apply to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025. Both replace the TIN language in mathematical-error section 6213(g)(2)(J) with social security number or employer identification number. The retained notice rules require an alleged error and explanation; the no-petition rule concerns a petition based on that notice. An abatement request may be filed within 60 days after the notice is sent. Receipt requires abatement; reassessment uses deficiency procedures and collection is stayed during the abatement period. No actual debt, wrongdoing, personal return or loss of every remedy is inferred. Selected House section 30001 replaces the current HEA 484(a)(5) student-aid status paragraph, with four distinct alternatives: a US citizen or national; an alien lawfully admitted for permanent residence under the INA; the specifically defined Cuban alternative; or an individual who lawfully resides in the United States in accordance with a COFA named by PRWORA 402(b)(2)(G). It does not impose a new US-residence condition common to all four alternatives. The Cuban branch has its own physical-presence condition, and the COFA branch has its own lawful-US-residence condition. The latter references the named Compacts, rather than importing all designated-benefit rules or territorial Governor options in section 402. Formal permanent-resident and US-national definitions retain their own scope; citizenship is not the only listed alternative. All five conditions of the Cuban alternative must hold. The alien must be a citizen or national of Cuba. The alien must be the beneficiary of an approved family-preference petition under INA 203(a). The alien must meet all immigrant-visa eligibility requirements while a visa is not immediately available. The alien must not otherwise be inadmissible under INA 212(a), with its own exceptions and references preserved. The alien must be physically present in the United States pursuant to a grant of parole in furtherance of the US minimum-annual-legal-migration commitment specified in the September 9, 1994 joint communique and reaffirmed in the May 2, 1995 joint statement. None of those conditions is replaced by nationality, any parole grant, an approved visa or the separate Cuban/Haitian-entrant category used elsewhere in the package. Complete family-preference allocation and inadmissibility text are bound as references, without determining anyone's petition, visa availability or admissibility. Existing parole authority is discretionary, temporary and case by case for the named purposes; parole is not admission and retains its own refugee limitation. This amendment does not itself grant parole, permanent residence, citizenship or a visa. The officially archived May 1995 statement describes its own conditional counting of specified Guantanamo humanitarian paroles toward the migration commitment; that does not make the House's five conditions optional or grant student assistance. Original September 1994 agreement acquisition and individual grant-to-agreement matching remain unfinished research, rather than unavailable evidence or an accepted programme classifier. No statement about the present operation or validity of those policies is made. The pre-vote 484(a) status paragraph separately allowed citizens/nationals, permanent residents, or the named INS-evidence branch for a non-temporary US purpose with intention of becoming a citizen or permanent resident. This is a statutory prerequisite, not an inferred motive of any individual or politician. House replaces that paragraph, not every Title IV condition or every source of educational funding. Complete current 484 governs receipt of grants, loans or work assistance under its own Title IV subchapter. Enrollment/credential/institution, satisfactory progress, prior debt/refund, educational-purpose/student-number certification and named prior-fraud repayment prerequisites remain with their own applicability. Loan/half-time/preparatory/teacher-credential, no-high-school/career-pathway, correspondence/distance, study-abroad and other special rules remain. No status label alone establishes all assistance conditions, and no private, State or universal scholarship ban is inferred. Retained immigration verification requires the named statements and supporting documentation, if required, before receipt; agency data matching is authorized. The printed review paragraph separately describes reasonable opportunity and pending-verification protections under its own conditions, with the institution enforcement and already-paid loan-guarantee boundaries retained. Current (g)(2) is a work-study-document special rule, while (g)(4) still prints documentation references to (2) and (2)(A). Their precise application is reserved as question 41; the original references and agency wording are not silently repaired or replaced with a guaranteed delay-to-loss interval. Own section 484(a)(4) student SSN certification and (o) verification/error/pending and guarantee conditions remain, rather than importing the education-tax-credit defined-SSN rule. A pending verification is not an adverse final determination or wrongdoing. The current intellectual-disability path retains its separate programme/progress requirements and expressly requires paragraphs (a)(3), (4), (5) and (6); its own limited waiver authority is not blanket personal eligibility. The confined-student Pell paragraph prints notwithstanding subsection (a), otherwise meets the subchapter eligibility requirements, and enrollment or acceptance in a prison education programme. Question 42 reserves exact interaction with the new (a)(5) before any individual exception or universal status-based denial for that path. The separate incarcerated-loan restriction is not a denial of every Pell award. These sources preserve the original applicable restrictions and exceptions without adjudicating an individual. House prints an effective date of July 1, 2025, applying to award year 2025-2026 and each subsequent award year. Current HEA 481 defines the award year as July 1 through June 30 of the following year, distinct from its academic-year definition and from taxable years in the education-credit sections. This is the May House action's proposed mechanism, without a claim that the House-only clause became law. It does not substitute current student aid into the frozen August 5, 1997 tax-credit references or establish a Senate counterpart. Other aid/package components remain unfinished. Selected House child and family funding clauses remain distinct appropriations and purposes. House 70109 adds $20 million for fiscal year 2025 to ICE, available until September 30, 2029. Those funds may only maintain care and custody during the pending charge and detain the alien with the alien's child. Both personal conditions must hold: the alien is charged only with a misdemeanor under INA 275(a), and entered the United States with the alien's child who has not attained 18 years. The pending-charge period is not every immigration proceeding or permanent detention. The complete entry statute distinguishes first and subsequent commissions and its other provisions; a charge is not a conviction, every alleged entry violation or proof of wrongdoing. This clause concerns an accompanied child and the charged parent, distinct from the UAC definition and funding below. It does not establish actual co-detention or a universal family entitlement. House 70115 separately adds $3 billion for fiscal year 2025 to ORR, available until September 30, 2029, only to house, transport and supervise unaccompanied alien children in ORR custody pursuant to TVPRA 235. The existing UAC definition requires no lawful US immigration status and age under 18; additionally there must either be no US parent/legal guardian, or no such person available to provide care and physical custody. Childhood, entry, or a parent elsewhere does not alone establish the category. The existing child-protection statute also retains its rule that a State agency or State-court-appointed person/entity acting in loco parentis is not a legal guardian for those specified sections. No individual category, new detention mandate, release decision or actual expenditure is inferred. House 70116 adds a separate $20 million to CBP for fiscal year 2025, available until September 30, 2029, only to examine a UAC who has attained 12 and is encountered by CBP for gang-related tattoos or markings. House 70117 adds another $20 million to ORR on the same fiscal/availability dates, only for the purpose of the TVPRA 235(c)(2)(A) danger-to-self-or-others determination by such an examination of each UAC who has attained 12. The CBP-encounter predicate is not silently imported into the ORR clause. Attainment of 12 is required by both clauses, distinct from the under-18 UAC definition. An examination or marking is not an automatic gang-membership, dangerousness, guilt or secure-placement finding. The material pre-vote placement rule requires prompt least-restrictive placement in the child's best interest, with danger and flight considerations permitted. Secure placement requires its own determination of danger to self or others, or a charge of a criminal offense, and has at-least-monthly review. The new funding does not itself decide any child's placement or erase these retained predicates. House 70118 adds $50 million to ORR for fiscal year 2025, available until September 30, 2029. Before placing a UAC with an individual under TVPRA 235(c), HHS must provide DHS the listed information concerning that individual and all adult household residents: names, SSNs, dates of birth, validated residence where the child will be placed, immigration status, contact information, and all background/criminal-check results. The minimum checks are the named public-records sex-offender registry, public-records background check and fingerprint-based national criminal-history check. This is a separate before-placement information duty, not either sponsor fee, an automatic immigration-status disqualification, or a finding that a sponsor/resident committed a crime. Current suitability and identity/relationship verification, independent child-risk finding and specified home studies remain material. Existing DHS-to-HHS database assistance on request is distinct from this HHS-to-DHS disclosure. No actual sponsor approval or disclosure is asserted. House 70119 adds $100 million to DHS for fiscal year 2025, available until September 30, 2029, only to permit a specified UAC to withdraw the admission application under INA 235(a)(4). The child may be from a contiguous or non-contiguous country. All printed case-by-case DHS determinations must hold: an immigration officer found the child at a US land border or port of entry and the child is inadmissible; the child has not been a victim of severe trafficking and there is no credible evidence of trafficking risk on return; and the child has no fear of return owing to a credible fear of persecution. These are conjunctive predicates, not every child encounter, non-citizenship or a universal repatriation mandate. The defined severe-trafficking reference retains its own sex/labor alternatives; no individual trafficking or fear finding is made. INA 235(a)(4) permits withdrawal and immediate departure at the named authority's discretion; funding is not actual permission, an admission decision or a removal order. Full current TVPRA 235 separately requires an independent-decision finding for its contiguous-country withdrawal path, alongside no-trafficking/no-credible-fear conditions, screening within 48 hours and before return, and transfer if criteria fail or cannot be determined in time. Its other-child care/transfer, removal proceedings, conditional counsel and safe-return protections remain source-bound; the general transfer period is 72 hours after UAC determination except exceptional circumstances. House 70119 explicitly covers both country groups and does not print that independent-decision condition. Question 43 reserves the precise interaction with those retained protections before an individual return pathway or a claim they were repealed. No unstated repeal or settlement of voluntariness/counsel/proceeding application is made. The selected funding is not a new blanket right to counsel, automatic eligibility or proof of any observed child outcome. Other enforcement/package provisions remain unfinished. Selected House ICE personnel and operational funding remains separate from the child, detention-capacity and fee clauses. House 70102 adds $858 million to ICE for fiscal year 2025, available until September 30, 2029. ICE may provide retention bonuses to an agent, officer or attorney committing to two additional years of immigration-enforcement service. It shall provide a signing bonus to each such person both hired on or after enactment and committing to five years of that service. Retention is permissive and the signing language mandatory for its defined group; neither establishes an actual bonus. The service-agreement paragraph requires the service-period dates or their determination, bonus amount, other payment conditions and early-termination conditions/effect. That paragraph prints U.S. Customs and Immigration Enforcement, whereas the surrounding appropriation and bonus clauses name U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Question 44 preserves that original entity wording and reserves exact application rather than silently repairing it or inventing an operating agency. House 70103 adds $8 billion to ICE for fiscal year 2025, available until September 30, 2029, only to hire additional officers, agents and support staff for immigration enforcement and prioritize/streamline retired ICE personnel hiring. It prints minima of 2,500 individuals hired in fiscal year 2025 and 1,875 in each named year 2026, 2027, 2028 and 2029. The later entries print the year without repeating fiscal year; they are preserved without converting them into a different calendar. These are proposed hiring requirements, not achieved hires or current workforce numbers. House 70104 separately adds $600 million for recruitment, hiring and onboarding capability, including IT, recruitment, marketing and necessary staff. House 70105 adds $14.4 billion only for transportation/removal operations and ensuring alien departure. House 70106 adds $700 million only for enforcement/removal IT, including fine and penalty collections; 70107 adds $550 million only for related facility upgrades; 70108 adds $250 million only for related fleet modernization. Each is additional fiscal year 2025 ICE funding available until September 30, 2029, with its own restricted purposes, not a single unrestricted account or actual expenditure. Funding transportation, collections or capacity is not a new removal ground, individual order, debt or observed enforcement result. House 70110 adds $650 million to ICE for fiscal year 2025, available until September 30, 2029, only to facilitate and implement INA 287(g) agreements. Complete pre-vote 287(g) permits the named authority to make written State/local agreements for qualified officers to perform the specified immigration functions, at State/local expense and consistently with State/local law. It requires knowledge/adherence to relevant federal law and written training certification, federal direction/supervision, and specified powers, duties, duration and supervisor. It preserves agreement conditions for federal property use, federal-employee displacement prohibition, limited federal-employee treatment and civil-liability/immunity rules. This funding is not a blanket deputization or amendment of those conditions, and no actual agreement, arrest, reimbursement or legal immunity is determined. House 70112 adds $1.32 billion to ICE for fiscal year 2025, available until September 30, 2029, only to hire OPLA attorneys/support staff to represent DHS in removal proceedings. House 70113 separately adds $500 million to DHS on those dates only for return under INA 235(b)(2)(C). The complete material paragraph covers the specified admission applicant arriving by land from contiguous foreign territory, whether or not at a designated port, and permits return to that territory pending the 1229a proceeding. Its parent paragraph and exceptions for crewman, covered expedited-removal applicant and stowaway remain; this is not every arriving alien, a compulsory return or permanent removal instead of that proceeding. House 70114 separately adds $787 million to ICE on those dates only for the named anti-gang/organization, domestic smuggling/trafficking, immigration-enforcement and State/local participation reimbursement purposes. Such stated purposes are not an allegation about any person or a new State/local removal authority. Other enforcement and package components remain unfinished. Selected House CBP and training-centre operations remain distinct appropriations. House 60002 adds fiscal year 2025 funds available until September 30, 2029: $4.1 billion to the CBP Commissioner to hire/train additional Border Patrol, Field Operations, Air and Marine, rehired-annuitant and support personnel; $2,052,630,000 for annual retention or signing bonuses for the named eligible agents/officers; $813 million to lease/acquire additional marked patrol units; and $600 million for border-workforce marketing, recruitment, applicant sourcing/vetting and operational mobility. Its processing-coordinator restriction applies to recruiting, hiring or training with subsection (a) personnel funds, without a printed start date.
