The complete incorporated definitions preserve unchanged lawful permanent residence and US national meaning, the referenced Compacts and the distinct 501(e) entrant branches already source-bound in the SNAP component. Special entrant parole/subsequent special status retains its own service-time wording; OTHER Cuban/Haitian nationals require their own parole-with-no-other-acquired-INA-status OR removal-proceedings OR pending-asylum alternative AND no final, nonappealable, legally enforceable removal order. The no-order modifier is not transferred to every special-status case, and service-time wording does not prove the proposal's HAS BEEN GRANTED predicate. Complete pre-vote public-benefit restrictions and exceptions remain separate; the provision is not described as the first COFA framework or a categorical outcome for every refugee/asylee/parolee who may independently hold another listed status or qualify under an exception. The preserved (v)(2) exception requires ALL of emergency-treatment necessity, otherwise meeting State-plan eligibility with the named aid/SSI/supplement disregards, AND care not related to an organ transplant. The (v)(3) emergency definition includes emergency labor/delivery and the specified acute-severity/immediate-attention risk tests; it is not all medical care. Preserved (v)(4) is a STATE ELECTION for otherwise eligible LAWFULLY US-RESIDING children UNDER 21 and/or women in its printed pregnancy/60-day category, including its battered-individual reference, sponsor and ongoing lawful-residence verification rules. It is not automatic assistance for every child or pregnant person regardless of lawful residence, election or other eligibility. The printed (v)(4) category is not used to infer a universal postpartum cutoff or resolve every other coverage law. CHIP incorporates the new (v)(5) restriction EXCEPT in relation to payments for services under 2105(a)(1)(D)(ii), whose complete baseline concerns health-services initiatives to improve children's health, including targeted and other low-income children. This is not a pregnancy-only exception, every child's guaranteed coverage, or an exception for every CHIP expenditure. Complete 2107(e) and the expressly incorporated EAS71103(b) renumbering are bound before the further 71109(b) insertion; unrelated address/simultaneous-enrollment rules are not turned into immigration meanings. The section appropriates $15 million to CMS for fiscal 2026 implementation, available until expended, without establishing actual spending or benefit amounts. House section 44110's verification-period option and House section 44111's rate provision are not imported into this Senate clause. Senate section 71110 adds 1905(kk), beginning October 1, 2026: NOTWITHSTANDING (y) and (z), the matching percentage for payments for care/services described in 1903(v)(2), furnished to an alien described in 1903(v)(1), SHALL NOT EXCEED the percentage determined under 1905(b) FOR THAT STATE. It concerns that emergency-care payment category and its own described recipient, not every Medicaid service, an end to emergency eligibility or the House's specified-State 80-percent rule beginning a year later. Complete 1903(v)(2)/(3) retains emergency necessity AND otherwise State-plan eligibility with the named disregards AND no organ-transplant procedure, along with the printed emergency-condition definition. The reference to (v)(1) is retained rather than converted into an exhaustive immigration-status label. Complete pre-vote 1905(b)/(y)/(z) supplies the ordinary State percentage and enhanced expansion/early-expansion framework against which the cap is described. The (b) percentage is State-specific and includes its own statutory rules; no flat nationwide 50-percent cap, mandatory rate exactly equal to the ceiling or repeal of every other matching rule is inferred. The section also appropriates $1 million to CMS for fiscal year 2026 implementation, available until expended; this is an appropriation, not proven spending, a beneficiary payment or quantified savings. The earlier EAS section 71109 emergency exception is not erased by this matching-rate provision. Senate section 71201 proposes its own new Medicare status restriction and longer existing-enrollee transition. The new section 1899C makes a listed immigration/citizenship category NECESSARY for entitlement to or enrollment in Title XVIII benefits, subject to its own existing-enrollee transition; the list is not sufficient entitlement, an award or proof that a person satisfies all other Medicare requirements. It lists US citizen OR US national, lawful permanent residence under the INA, the version's own category(3), OR lawful US residence in accordance with a referenced Compact of Free Association. Unlike the new SNAP/Medicaid lists, 1899C(a) does not print a NEW COMMON RESIDENCE modifier across every alternative; the COFA alternative keeps its own lawful-residence predicate and other existing Medicare residence rules retain their own scopes. Complete material pre-vote 226/226A/1836 and 1818(a)/1818A(a) are bound. They distinguish hospital entitlement through the named age/insured-benefit, disability/railroad/government-employment or renal-disease pathways from separate Part B or premium Part A enrollment paths. In 1836(a), existing Part A entitlement is an ALTERNATIVE to the age 65/US-resident branch, whose citizen OR LPR alternatives have a five-year continuous-residence condition on the LPR branch. Complete 1818(a) has its own age 65, Part B enrollment, US residence, citizen OR LPR-with-five-years and no-other-Part-A-entitlement conjunction. The five-year modifier is not applied to every citizen, every enrollee or every entitlement path. The limited 1836(b) post-renal immunosuppressive-drug enrollment and own other-coverage exclusions remain distinct from full benefits. Complete 1818A(a) preserves its own disabled/earnings-related premium eligibility, not a generic disability guarantee. Neither age alone nor listed status alone is described as sufficient; the selected proposal does not directly rewrite each underlying benefit rule or establish an exhaustive pre-vote eligibility universe. The transition applies specifically to individuals ENTITLED TO OR ENROLLED FOR Title XVIII benefits AS OF ENACTMENT. The Commissioner must review that cohort to identify people not described in ANY of the four listed alternatives, and notify EACH identified person of termination at the enactment-relative date, as soon as practicable AFTER IDENTIFICATION and in a manner designed to ensure comprehension. The termination date is not measured from receipt or sending of the notice; the review deadline is not the termination date. No identical grace period is promised to every later applicant, perpetual grandfathering, actual completed review, actual termination or observed administrative outcome is inferred. Enactment-relative dates are not converted into dates based on this vote or the later enacted law. Senate category(3) instead requires an alien who HAS BEEN GRANTED Cuban and Haitian entrant status as defined in 501(e). The complete definition retains the special-parole/subsequent-special-status category's service-time wording, and the OTHER Cuban/Haitian-national category's (parole with NO other-acquired-INA-status OR removal proceedings OR pending asylum) AND NO final/nonappealable/legally-enforceable removal-order grouping. The no-order modifier stays in the latter category and the no-other-status modifier in its parole alternative; nationality or service-time wording does not prove an actual grant. House 203(a)-petition/visa/program predicates are not imported. The restriction applies to the existing-enrollee cohort EIGHTEEN MONTHS AFTER ENACTMENT, with review completed NOT LATER THAN ONE YEAR AFTER ENACTMENT and each identified person's comprehensible notice tied to that eighteen-month termination date. This is not an eighteen-month period from notice or a guarantee of six months between notice and termination. Senate sections 71301/71302 propose their own ACA status and special-income-rule changes. The selected ACA status provision adds lawfully present aliens who are NOT eligible aliens to 36B(e)(1), whose named condition concerns one or more individuals for whom the taxpayer is allowed a section 151 deduction (including taxpayer or spouse), and whose complete existing mechanism reduces the portion of counted premiums attributable to the affected INDIVIDUAL and adjusts family-size/household-income calculations using the specified fraction or comparable method. It is not automatic loss of every otherwise eligible household member's credit or a blanket ban on insurance enrollment. Existing 36B(e)(2) whole-period citizenship/nationality/lawful-presence wording is retained as subparagraph(A); the new eligible-alien provision concerns an individual who IS AN ALIEN AND LAWFULLY PRESENT and who IS, AND IS REASONABLY EXPECTED TO BE FOR THE ENTIRE CREDIT-ENROLLMENT PERIOD, within its own listed LPR, version-specific Cuban-related, OR COFA-lawful-residence category. Both current status and the reasonable whole-period expectation remain, common to the listed alternatives; a single day of status, nationality alone or any lawful temporary stay is not substituted. Citizens/US nationals are not required to fit the new alien-only list. Separate applicable-taxpayer, income, coverage-month, plan/enrollment and other credit requirements remain; status alone is not sufficient. The companion provision deletes 36B(c)(1)(B), whose complete pre-vote special rule requires ALL of household income NOT GREATER THAN 100 percent of the family poverty line, LAWFUL PRESENCE as an alien, AND Medicaid ineligibility BY REASON OF THAT ALIEN STATUS, then treats that taxpayer as applicable with income equal to 100 percent for credit purposes. It is not every Medicaid-ineligible person, any low income or a finding that the person lacks lawful presence. Deletion removes that special treatment for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025; it does not alone prove that EVERY person at EXACTLY 100 percent loses the credit, because ordinary (c)(1)(A) begins at 100 percent subject to its other rules. The temporary 2021-2025 upper-income rule and complete coverage predicates are separately bound, without extending it into future years or quantifying an actual credit. The status provision's non-conforming amendments apply to TAXABLE YEARS BEGINNING AFTER DECEMBER 31, 2026; its conforming amendments apply to PLAN YEARS BEGINNING ON OR AFTER JANUARY 1, 2027. Those tax/plan-year bases remain distinct from the earlier special-rule repeal; neither vote date nor later enacted implementation dates are substituted. Both status versions replace the lawful-alien phrase in 5000A(d)(3) with the eligible-alien reference; they do NOT change the bound penalty calculation's existing zero-dollar/zero-percent components. No revived monetary mandate penalty or actual tax/benefit determination is inferred. Senate 36B(e)(2)(B) prints IF, preserving that wording rather than substituting the House IF AND ONLY IF. Its category(ii) requires HAS BEEN GRANTED defined Cuban/Haitian entrant status, subject to the same current status AND reasonable expectation for the entire credit-enrollment period. Complete 501(e) keeps special parole/subsequent special status distinct from OTHER Cuban/Haitian nationals whose own (parole-with-no-other-status OR removal-proceedings OR pending-asylum) alternatives share NO final/nonappealable/legally-enforceable removal order. Modifiers remain in their own branch; nationality/service-time wording does not establish a grant. No House family-petition/visa/parole-program conjunction is imported. Senate 71301 adds eligible-alien verification/attestation to the named 1411 provisions, but its (c)(1)(C) attestation extension concerns premium tax credits alone, where House text also names reduced cost-sharing. Its 1412(d) insertion concerns CREDITS UNDER 36B for aliens not eligible, where House text inserts a broader individual disqualifier into the federal-payments provision. It has no direct counterpart to the selected House 1402(e)/1331(e)(1) status amendments. Senate 71302 deletes 36B(c)(1)(B) without the House renumbering, basic-health branch removal or cost-sharing sentence deletion. The remaining pre-vote 1402(b) text references the removed 36B(c)(1)(B); application to residual cost-sharing/basic-health rules is separately reserved. Absence of direct Senate amendments does not prove continuing awards, automatic loss or resolved effects of those cross-references. General Exchange verification provisions are a separate description and do not become an insurance-enrollment ban through this credit-status summary. Senate section 71303 proposes its own Exchange premium-credit verification and filing-compliance conditions. The selected Exchange verification provision adds credit coverage-month conditions for an INDIVIDUAL enrolled in a qualified health plan through an Exchange. A month beginning BEFORE the specified verification is excluded unless the own past-month verification clause is met; this is not an assertion that all earlier months are permanently lost. Applicable information must be PROVIDED OR VERIFIED BY THE APPLICANT, with affirmation of at least the listed information TO THE EXTENT RELEVANT to the specified eligibility. Both versions expressly say failure of this paragraph ALONE does NOT make an individual ineligible to enroll through the Exchange for that month. Credit coverage-month, advance payment, reduced cost-sharing and enrollment are distinct; no insurance-enrollment ban, actual credit award/loss or guaranteed verification date is inferred. Both versions separately exclude a plan from the tax provision's qualified-health-plan definition UNLESS the Exchange PROVIDES a pre-enrollment verification PROCESS through which ANY APPLICANT MAY, BEGINNING NOT LATER THAN AUGUST 1, verify the version-specific information/eligibility for plans in the SUBSEQUENT PLAN YEAR. This is an Exchange process availability deadline, not a requirement that each applicant must submit or complete verification by August 1, a universal enrollment period or a promise of coverage. Amendments in these selected sections apply to TAXABLE YEARS BEGINNING AFTER DECEMBER 31, 2027; the incorporated Senate rule's post-2025 scope is not substituted as the statute's effective date. Senate coverage-month verification requires enrollment eligibility AND eligibility for ANY advance premium credit payment; it has NO House reduced-cost-sharing third prong. Its information list pairs HOUSEHOLD INCOME AND FAMILY SIZE and asks WHETHER THE INDIVIDUAL IS AN ELIGIBLE ALIEN, alongside coverage, residence and authorized other necessary information. Past-month verification prints IF, without importing the House IF AND ONLY IF, and retains own enrollment/advance-credit eligibility FOR THAT MONTH. The Secretary MAY waive ONLY subparagraph (A) for an individual enrolling for ONE OR MORE taxable-year months DURING an Exchange special enrollment period BASED ON CHANGE IN THAT INDIVIDUAL'S FAMILY SIZE; it is not an automatic waiver, every special enrollment period or a waiver of all other credit requirements. Exchanges may use ANY AVAILABLE DATA AND RELIABLE third-party sources in collecting information FOR VERIFICATION BY THE APPLICANT; permission does not make every third-party source reliable or eliminate applicant verification. The Senate filing-compliance clause names ONLY 45 CFR 155.305(f)(4)(iii) AS PUBLISHED JUNE 25, 2025 (90 FR 27074), APPLIED AS THOUGH TO ALL PLAN YEARS AFTER 2025. The final rule's printed (iii) says PLAN YEAR 2026 ONLY and supplies the one-year filing/reconciliation condition and its own tax-information-protecting notice alternatives; the bill expressly changes that referenced duration. The rule's separate introductory two-consecutive-year baseline is not substituted for the named (iii), nor is the House March proposal. The condition retains HHS notification, prior advances for filer OR married-couple spouse, the year whose tax data would be used, and failure to file/reconcile for that period. Direct failure notification to the filer OR indirect risk/education notification to filer/enrollee remains; there is no guarantee of a fixed notice-to-loss interval. The Senate pre-enrollment process covers verification of the applicant's HOUSEHOLD INCOME AND ELIGIBILITY FOR ENROLLMENT for the subsequent plan year, without importing the House advance-credit/cost-sharing list. This section has no direct counterpart to the selected House 44201(b)(1) statutory missing-data/discrepancy additions. Absence of that direct amendment does not establish that no other verification rules apply or that the House exception determines Senate awards. Residual program/application questions remain separately reserved. The Senate ACA candidate now binds the complete pre-vote cost-sharing credit dependency identified by independent source-completeness review. Complete pre-vote section 1402(g) adds a material boundary to the selected ACA cost-sharing comparison: NO cost-sharing reduction is allowed for coverage for ANY MONTH UNLESS that month is a COVERAGE MONTH FOR WHICH A SECTION 36B CREDIT IS ALLOWED TO THE INSURED OR AN APPLICABLE TAXPAYER ON THE INSURED'S BEHALF. This is a necessary credit/month dependency, not a sufficient entitlement, and it does not require every insured to be the tax filer personally. Shared terms take section 36B meanings; eligibility data use the taxable year of the ADVANCE DETERMINATION, not the taxable year for which the credit is allowed. Retaining a cost-sharing sentence or basic-health branch alone therefore does not establish continuing reductions or an award. Individual/family calculations, own program predicates and the direct House/Senate amendment distinctions remain; residual cross-reference/program application stays RESERVED as question 34. No individual credit, reduction or basic-health outcome is adjudicated. Senate section 70604 proposes a 1 PERCENT remittance tax under its own physical-funding and noncash provisions. Both selected remittance sections require the SENDER to pay the tax, the PROVIDER to collect it FROM THE SENDER AND remit QUARTERLY as prescribed by the Secretary, and secondary provider liability ONLY TO THE EXTENT the tax is unpaid at transfer AND not collected. These are separate payer, collection and secondary-liability roles, not a tax only on providers or a charge already observed. Both deem the remittance a financing transaction for the specified multiple-party anti-conduit authority; existing 7701(l) permits appropriate regulation/recharacterization, not an automatic finding of evasion or wrongdoing. Transfer amendments apply to TRANSFERS MADE AFTER DECEMBER 31, 2025, not the vote date or a substituted later enacted date. The bound remittance definitions concern an ELECTRONIC, PROVIDER-INITIATED funds transfer requested by a CONSUMER/NATURAL-PERSON SENDER LOCATED IN A DEFINED STATE to an AUTHORIZED DESIGNATED RECIPIENT LOCATED IN A FOREIGN COUNTRY. Consumer/State, electronic and normal-course provider definitions are independently bound, with account-independence and the statutory SMALL-VALUE EXCLUSION retained. This is not every domestic payment, every cross-border business transaction, every family expense or a recipient-citizenship test. Electronic transfer technology and the Senate physical FUNDING instrument are different predicates. No specific transaction, person, provider, regulatory threshold or actual tax outcome is classified. The Senate tax applies ONLY where the sender provides CASH, MONEY ORDER, CASHIER'S CHECK OR ANOTHER SIMILAR PHYSICAL INSTRUMENT AS THE SECRETARY DETERMINES to the provider, and remains subject to its SEPARATE NONAPPLICATION provisions. Nonapplication covers funds WITHDRAWN FROM AN ACCOUNT held in/by an institution BOTH DESCRIBED IN 31 USC 5312(a)(2)(A)-(H) AND SUBJECT TO SUBCHAPTER II OF CHAPTER 53 requirements, OR funds PROVIDED WITH A DEBIT OR CREDIT CARD ISSUED IN THE US. The listed-institution AND regulatory-subjection conditions are conjunctive; not every institution or any card regardless of issuance suffices. Cash-only language is not used to erase a separately applicable nonapplication or classify intermediate withdrawals/funding paths. Complete debit/card definitions retain network/asset-account and no-paper-check scope; the bill says WITHOUT REGARD TO debit-definition (B), rather than an automatic exclusion of every possible prepaid card. The inherited credit-device definition is separately bound, with the US-issuance condition additional. The Senate prints EFTA 919(g) for remittance and 920(c)(2)/(3) for card definitions, matching the bound source-credit crosswalk; it has no counterpart to the selected House verified citizen/national-provider exception, new 36C credit or 6050BB reporting scheme. Those missing counterparts do not establish a citizenship-based Senate tax exemption or a person's final cost. All own funding/exclusion and statutory-definition predicates must be retained; no universal 1% charge on all remittances or outcome for a particular immigrant is inferred. The selected Senate ACA comparison remains its own 71301/71302/71303 eligible-alien, income-floor and verification mechanisms described above, with their respective tax/plan-year dates. Their complete operative sections do not contain the House 44201(i) named-June-2012-DACA amendments. No House title-wide, cost-sharing-section or preceding-Federal-payment-sentence exclusion is imported into those Senate clauses, and their own eligible-alien restrictions remain. This selected-section comparison does not claim Senate eligibility for every DACA recipient or whole-package absence of every possible DACA effect; the original memo is not a current ACA eligibility decision. Selected Senate section 70104 requires the qualifying child's defined SSN in either case. The taxpayer must also include the taxpayer's defined SSN or, on a joint return, the defined SSN of at least one spouse. This is not both spouses on every joint return, a child SSN alone, or a grant to every mixed-status household. It does not add the House SIMILAR-32(d) clause, so that new House marital rule is not imported. Its amendments apply to TAXABLE YEARS BEGINNING AFTER DECEMBER 31, 2024. Full section context extends 24(h), prints $2,200 rather than the House temporary $2,500/later $2,000 structure, and uses its own after-2025 credit-amount inflation with base-year substitution and rounding. Own refundable ceiling/inflation and the underlying credit conditions remain; no actual indexed amount/refund is calculated. Selected same-bill 70103 zero-exemption extension retains the reference rule, with its own after-2024 date; its separate senior-deduction/SSN mechanism is addressed below. The child-credit comparison is with the complete pre-vote 24(a)-(h), not its separate historical 2021 regime. Before either amendment, 24(h)(7) required the QUALIFYING CHILD'S defined SSN; the new clauses add claimant-side conditions without changing that child prerequisite. An SSN is not alone citizenship proof. Both new definitions permit SSA issuance to either a US citizen or an individual under the named work-authorized-alien branch, including the specified catch-up portion. In either case, the SSN must have been issued before the due date for the return. Any other SSA issuance purpose or an ITIN does not alone satisfy this definition. Complete SSA issuance text distinguishes those branches. Section 24(c) retains an incorporated 152(c) qualifying child AND its own NOT-ATTAINED-17 requirement and its separate citizenship/residence limitation; complete 152 preserves relationship, abode/support, joint-return/refund, competing-claim, adopted/foster, custody/release and missing-child exceptions. Neither a valid SSN nor a citizenship label establishes all credit prerequisites. Own income/phaseout, earned-income/refund, tax/identification/year and other conditions remain; credit/refund figures are not guaranteed payments. Retained 24(h)(4) is separate: (A) provides a $500 other-dependent branch with own (B) noncitizen boundary, and (C) says a qualifying child not allowed credit BY REASON OF PARAGRAPH (7) is treated as a dependent to whom (A) applies. Neither bill strikes that text. Its application to newly added taxpayer/spouse SSN failures is RESERVED as question 39; no automatic fallback award, complete household-credit loss or claim about every dependent is made. Pre-vote 151(d)(5)(B) says reducing the exemption amount to zero is NOT TAKEN INTO ACCOUNT in determining allowed/allowable/entitled deductions for OTHER TITLE PROVISIONS, so zero exemptions alone do not establish no child credit. The exact same-bill 151(d)(5) amendments extend the zero-exemption period while retaining that reference rule; distinct own dates and separately addressed Senate senior provisions are not merged into this child-credit description. Both amend 6213(g)(2)(I) from section 24(e) to SECTION 24 for omission of a correct identification number; this mathematical-or-clerical-error mechanism is not a finding of fraud, corruption, an actual debt or removal of all remedies. Complete 6213(b)(1)/(2) requires notice of the alleged error AND explanation, distinguishes that notice from a deficiency notice/no petition BASED ON THAT NOTICE, permits an abatement request WITHIN 60 DAYS AFTER NOTICE IS SENT, requires abatement UPON RECEIPT of that request, subjects reassessment to deficiency procedures and stays levy/court collection during the abatement period. No actual notice, filing deadline, assessment, successful claim or taxpayer classification is inferred. Senate section 70103 adds its own section 151(d)(5)(C) deduction of $6,000 for each qualified individual in a taxable year beginning before January 1, 2029, subject to its effective date for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024. There are two listed person alternatives: the taxpayer, or the taxpayer's spouse on a joint return. In either case, the claimed person must have attained 65 before the tax year closes and that person's defined SSN must be included on the return. One spouse's number alone does not establish deductions for both seniors. The amount is reduced, but not below zero, by 6 percent of modified adjusted gross income over $75,000, or over $150,000 on a joint return. If the taxpayer is married within the meaning of section 7703, this subparagraph applies only if the taxpayer and spouse file a joint return. The new House similar-32(d) provision and hypothetical-itemizer mechanism are not imported. This own deduction accompanies the extended zero-exemption/reference rules rather than replacing every existing aged standard amount or exempting all Social Security income. The inherited SSN definition is the same version's amended section 24(h)(7). It permits SSA issuance to either a US citizen or an individual under the named work-authorized-alien branch, including the specified catch-up portion. In either case, the number must have been issued before the due date for the return. An ITIN or any other SSA number does not alone satisfy the definition, and the listed alien branch is not citizenship-only. The child-credit joint-return alternative does not replace the senior deduction's identification condition. Full marital authorities retain their own reference scopes and conditional separated-spouse rules; this description does not determine anyone's marital status. Complete section 63 preserves taxable-income and itemization mechanics and its own standard-deduction exclusions, including a nonresident alien individual. Section 151 retains its own spouse/exemption references and zero-exemption rule for other-provision deduction references. These are source-bound prerequisites, rather than eligibility for every alien, senior or itemizer or an accepted override of an exclusion. A deduction is not a dollar-for-dollar credit, an exemption of all Social Security benefits or a guaranteed refund. Both versions' senior amendments apply to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024. Each version retains its own printed limit for a taxable year beginning before January 1, 2029. Both modified-income definitions add amounts excluded under sections 911, 931 and 933. No personal amount, return, age, marriage, residency or tax outcome is determined. Each adds its own mathematical-error omission reference: House (Z) names its section 63(f)(5)(D), while Senate (W) names its section 151(d)(5)(C). Those labels and provisions are not interchangeable. The inherited notice rules require an alleged error and explanation; the no-petition rule concerns a petition based on that notice. An abatement request may be filed within 60 days after the notice is sent. On receipt of that request the assessment must be abated, any reassessment uses deficiency procedures, and levy/court collection is stayed during the abatement period. No actual debt, fraud or loss of every remedy is inferred. Selected Senate section 70606 requires the individual's defined SSN on the return for both education credits. If the credit concerns qualified tuition and related expenses of an individual other than the taxpayer or spouse, that other individual's name and defined SSN are also required. The individual-number requirement applies in either expense case. It does not add the House conditional spouse-number clause or the House amendment to section 25A(g)(6). The retained married-individual rule applies only if a taxpayer married within section 7703 files a joint return with the spouse. Absence of a new spouse-number clause is not separate-return eligibility, and the child-credit at-least-one-spouse alternative is not an education-credit rule. Both selected education sections replace section 25A(g)(1), whose subsection (a) covers the American Opportunity Tax Credit and Lifetime Learning Credit. Before amendment, the general student name and taxpayer-identification-number rule applied to both credits, while the additional student/taxpayer issuance-date and institution-number rules were AOTC-specific. The new defined-SSN condition applies to both credits. Both inherit their own same-bill amended section 24(h)(7) definition: SSA issuance to either a US citizen or the named work-authorized-alien branch, including its specified catch-up portion. In either case, the number must have been issued before the return due date. Any SSA number or an ITIN does not alone meet that definition; it is not citizenship-only. The old AOTC student deadline says on or before the due date, while the new definition says before. Those exact bounds are preserved. Child-credit claimant alternatives and senior each-person rules do not replace the education section's named roles. Both new institution clauses concern only the American Opportunity Tax Credit: the taxpayer must include the employer identification number of any institution to which the taxpayer paid qualified tuition and related expenses taken into account under section 25A on the tax-year return. That is not a new institution-number requirement for Lifetime Learning or for every institution irrespective of the named payments. Expenses paid by a qualifying dependent retain section 25A(g)(3)'s treatment as paid by the other taxpayer; the dependent cannot independently claim the credit under that paragraph. Full dependent and zero-exemption reference conditions remain, without an individual family determination. Material credit prerequisites remain. AOTC has its per-student, election, four-prior-year, first-four-postsecondary-years, eligible-academic-period, half-time and named felony-drug/prior-claim restrictions. Lifetime Learning has its per-taxpayer expense and job-skills/course context. Own income phaseouts, excluded-income additions, expense definitions and nonacademic/sports exclusions, assistance reductions, prepayments, double-benefit prohibition, payee-statement exception, partial-AOTC-refund/child restriction and recapture authority remain. A defined number is necessary under the new identification clause, rather than proof of all student, expense, credit or refund prerequisites. The AOTC eligible-student reference names HEA 484(a)(1), as in effect when section 25A was enacted, and separately requires at least half the normal full-time course load. It does not name the whole of current 484(a), including its separate citizenship paragraph. The institution definition separately requires the frozen HEA 481 description and eligibility to participate in a title IV program. Code reference notes identify the frozen date as August 5, 1997. Historical 1996 and 1997 witnesses preserve the selected student enrollment/credential provision, its preparatory-course and teacher-credential exceptions, and the complete referenced institution conditions, including their incorporated historical definitions. Selected student and incorporated institution-definition passages match exactly; full HEA 481 operative words match only after two declared split-word comparisons. Original texts remain unchanged. Annual dates alone do not establish personal or institutional eligibility, and neither current student-aid eligibility nor a new House student-aid provision is silently substituted for those frozen tax references. The retained nonresident rule applies if the taxpayer was a nonresident alien for any portion of the tax year. Section 25A applies only if that individual is treated as a resident for chapter 1 by a section 6013(g) or (h) election. The (g) path requires the named nonresident individual at year close to be married to a citizen or resident and both spouses to make the election. Its duration, neither-spouse-resident nonapplication, termination and re-election limits remain. The (h) path requires nonresident status at year beginning, resident status at year close, marriage at year close to a citizen or resident, and both individuals' prescribed election; its own one-election limit remains. Tax-resident treatment for the specified chapters does not grant immigration status, work authorization, citizenship or a credit automatically. This is not a categorical denial to every noncitizen. Both sections apply to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025. Both replace the TIN language in mathematical-error section 6213(g)(2)(J) with social security number or employer identification number. The retained notice rules require an alleged error and explanation; the no-petition rule concerns a petition based on that notice. An abatement request may be filed within 60 days after the notice is sent. Receipt requires abatement; reassessment uses deficiency procedures and collection is stayed during the abatement period. No actual debt, wrongdoing, personal return or loss of every remedy is inferred. Selected Senate 100052(8) uses the $29.85 billion additional fiscal year 2025 ICE appropriation, available through September 30, 2029, for its listed purposes; it does not earmark the entire account or a separate House $20 million for family unity. Its family-unity purpose maintains care and custody during the pending specified charge, expressly in accordance with applicable laws, and detains the alien with the alien's child. Both conditions must hold: the alien is charged only with a misdemeanor under INA 275(a), and entered the United States with the alien's child who has not attained 18 years. The charge is not a conviction or proof of wrongdoing; the complete entry statute distinguishes its own first/subsequent and other provisions. This is the selected accompanied-parent/child funding purpose, not all family detention, the UAC category or actual co-detention. The express applicable-laws wording is preserved for this Senate clause without adding it to the House printed clause or adjudicating either's legal constraints. House 70115-70119 UAC capacity, examinations, disclosure and withdrawal provisions are not substituted for this exact Senate family-unity purpose. Other enforcement/package components remain unfinished. Selected Senate 100052 personnel and operations purposes share the $29.85 billion additional fiscal year 2025 ICE account, available through September 30, 2029. They are not separate House account amounts or individual earmarks of the entire envelope. Paragraph (1) funds hiring and training additional officers, agents, investigators and support staff, prioritizing/streamlining retired ICE hires, without importing the House printed yearly hiring minima. Paragraph (2) permits the Director to give discretionary performance bonuses for exemplary service and retention bonuses for two additional years of enforcement service. Signing bonuses may go to an agent, officer or attorney both hired on or after enactment and committing to five years of that service. Unlike the House signing clause, this is may, not shall. A retention/signing bonus requires the written service-period/amount/payment/early-termination agreement, with its own terms. No bonus, hiring or exemplary-performance outcome is inferred. Paragraph (3) supports recruitment/hiring/onboarding through IT, recruitment/marketing and necessary staff. Paragraph (4) funds transportation and related costs associated with departure or removal operations. Paragraphs (5)-(7) fund enforcement/removal IT including fee collections, facility upgrades and fleet modernization. The Senate fee-collection wording is not replaced by House fine-and-penalty wording; funding does not establish actual fees collected, debts or removal orders. Paragraph (9) funds expanding, facilitating and implementing 287(g) agreements; full material pre-vote qualification/training/law/supervision/written-power/duration/voluntary and other agreement limits remain, with State/local expense and own communication/cooperation alternatives preserved. No blanket deputization or new State removal authority follows from funding. Paragraph (10) funds VOICE staffing/training and nonfinancial assistance to victims of crimes perpetrated by aliens present without authorization. This is the stated conditional purpose, not a finding that any person committed a crime, that status alone proves wrongdoing, or that every victim receives cash. Paragraph (11) funds OPLA attorneys/support staff representing DHS in immigration enforcement and removal proceedings, preserving the Senate scope rather than the House removal-only purpose. Each remains a funding purpose, not an observed workforce, crime, representation, agreement or expenditure. Previously reviewed family-unity paragraph (8) retains its separate conditions. Other package components remain unfinished. Selected Senate CBP operations use their own account and temporal rules. Senate 90002(a)(1) adds $4.1 billion for fiscal year 2025 CBP hiring/training, including field support personnel; (2) adds $2,052,630,000 for eligible recruitment bonuses, performance awards or annual retention bonuses; and (3) adds $855 million for existing patrol-unit repair and additional-unit lease/acquisition, without the House marked-only word. Each of those three paragraphs expressly remains available until September 30, 2029. Paragraph (4) separately adds $5 billion for lease, acquisition, construction, design or improvement of facilities and checkpoints owned, leased or operated by CBP but does not print the same until-September-2029 phrase. Question 45 reserves its precise availability application; that date is not silently extended to (4), nor is a different expiry assumed. Subsection (b) prohibits using subsection (a) funds to recruit, hire or train processing-coordinator personnel after October 31, 2028, not an immediate blanket coordinator ban or a repeal of the funded screening purposes. The House restriction scope/date and ICE bonus service conditions are not substituted. Senate 90004 adds $6.168 billion for fiscal year 2025 CBP purposes, available until September 30, 2029, as one listed-purpose envelope rather than House separate technology earmarks. Its purposes include nonintrusive equipment/related technology for narcotics entry or exit at ports and named borders; Air/Marine platforms; surveillance; referenced biometric entry/exit; screening persons entering or exiting; initial UAC screening consistent with TVPRA; border/drug trafficking efforts; and commemorations. Its tower restriction applies to subsection (a) funds for towers along the southwest and northern borders: the same tower must have both been tested and been accepted by CBP to deliver autonomous capabilities. It does not print the House Federal-Government accepting authority or the same fund/geographic scope. The Senate autonomous definition concerns a system designed for algorithmic real-time detection, identification, classification and tracking and operational adjustments without active/continuous human control. This is a definition/procurement boundary, not proven capability, a new adjudication rule or a guarantee against errors. Complete material biometric-system authority retains its original data-category, accuracy/access/misuse/correction/appeals and other conditions, without a new every-traveller biometric mandate or actual immigration outcome from funding. Initial UAC screening retains the full statutory UAC definition and is expressly consistent with TVPRA. Full material child-screening, transfer and placement protections remain bound; this does not import House age-12 tattoo examinations, sponsor disclosure or disputed withdrawal application, establish an actual finding, or create universal child detention/return. Senate 90007 separately adds DHS $10 billion for fiscal year 2025, available until September 30, 2029, to reimburse costs of activities supporting the named border-safeguarding mission. It does not itself state a State-only beneficiary or the distinct other reimbursement sections' January date; those mechanisms are not merged, and no actual reimbursement or new enforcement power follows. Senate 100053 separately adds DHS/FLETC $750 million for fiscal year 2025, available until September 30, 2029. Not less than $285 million is for training newly hired Federal law enforcement personnel employed by DHS and State and local law enforcement agencies operating in support of DHS. Not more than $465 million is for the listed facility procurement/construction/maintenance/improvement/training-equipment/related expenses. These are a training floor and facilities ceiling within the envelope, not two exact House-sized earmarks; the training categories and facility purposes retain their own Senate scope. All selected funding remains proposed appropriations/purposes, not observed hires, awards, training, data outcomes, costs reimbursed or actual expenditures. Other agency/enforcement and package components remain unfinished. Selected Senate 100054 EOIR, State/local grants and incarceration purposes share the additional $3.33 billion fiscal year 2025 DOJ account, available through September 30, 2029. This is a multi-purpose envelope, not the entire amount earmarked for any selected purpose or the separate House $1.25 billion/$950 million allocations. Paragraph (1) funds immigration judges/support to address the petitions/cases/removals backlog. Effective November 1, 2028, it states EOIR shall comprise not more than 800 immigration judges plus necessary support. That is a proposed ceiling and effective date, not a target minimum, actual workforce, inferred number of cuts or proven backlog change. Paragraph (7) covers the specified State/political-subdivision incarceration compensation and its complete eligibility/limitation. The new incarceration-compensation criteria require a felony conviction or at least two misdemeanor convictions in every listed case. In addition, one of three alternatives must hold. The alien entered without inspection or at a time or place not designated by DHS. Alternatively, the alien was subject to removal proceedings when taken into State/local custody. Alternatively, the alien was admitted as a nonimmigrant and, at that custody time, failed to maintain the admitted or changed nonimmigrant status or comply with its conditions. Those entry/proceeding/status alternatives do not remove the common conviction requirement; a charge, one misdemeanor, any noncitizen status or mere encounter is not substituted. They do not themselves establish a new crime, removal ground or individual custody/status/conviction finding. The compensation limitation excludes the State/local entity if it prohibits or in any way restricts the specified federal/State/local personnel from any of the listed activities: immigration-law compliance; federal-enforcement assistance/cooperation; or the named citizenship/status/admissibility/deportability/custody-information inquiries, federal encounter notifications or responses to federal information requests. The incorporated immigration-laws definition includes its named laws, conventions and treaties; it is not new independent State removal authority. This is the printed funding limitation, not a finding that any State is disqualified, a label for every local policy or a conclusion about constitutional enforceability. Complete pre-vote INA 241(i) already provides its own State-incarceration route after a chief-executive written request, with an AG-determined compensation contract or federal-custody alternative, average-cost basis, complete criminal/status definition, priority/security provisions and dated authorization/correctional-purpose limits. Its original exclusion/deportation and Attorney General wording is preserved, distinct from the new removal/DHS wording. No first-ever compensation authority, actual contract/award or current appropriation is inferred. Those old-route fields are not silently imported as new conditions of the self-contained House or Senate funding paragraphs. Paragraph (5) funds the named Byrne Justice Assistance Grant and COPS initiatives associated with violent-crime investigation/prosecution, criminal enforcement, and immigration enforcement/removal. Its located limitation says funds under this subsection shall not be available to community violence intervention/prevention initiatives. Its located eligibility clause requires State/local government full compliance with 1373, as determined by the AG. Paragraph (7)(C) says amounts under this subsection shall be distributed to more than one State, then excludes its subparagraph (A) compensation for the specified entity restrictions. The section is organized as numbered purposes rather than an expressly lettered subsection. Question 46 reserves the exact scope of those under-this-subsection references before assuming they apply only to the neighboring purpose or to the entire $3.33 billion envelope. Original words and locations are preserved, not repaired into a settled scope. Complete material 1373 retains its own prohibition on restricting the specified government sending/receiving, requesting, maintaining and exchanging status information, plus the named agency inquiry response for a purpose authorized by law. Original INS wording and transfer note remain, without a State-compliance finding, newly unlimited data access, general arrest duty, individual status determination or constitutional/enforceability acceptance. Funding/grant conditions are not a new immigration crime or State removal power. Other DOJ purposes, reimbursement/removal and package components remain unfinished; no actual grant, incarceration compensation, judge staffing or observed enforcement result. Selected Senate 100054(2) and (3) drug/prosecution purposes remain within the already described additional $3.33 billion fiscal year 2025 DOJ envelope through September 30, 2029, without importing House $500 million/$600 million earmarks. Paragraph (2) includes drug trafficking, fentanyl and its precursors, and illegal drug use; generic drug funding is not itself an immigration finding. Paragraph (3) names immigration matters, gang-related crimes involving aliens, child trafficking and smuggling involving aliens within the United States, unlawful voting by aliens, Alien Registration Act violations, and PRWORA title IV violations/fraud, including additional DOJ personnel to investigate/prosecute those matters. It prints unlawful voting, rather than the broader literal House voting wording, without creating a universal alien-voting prohibition or changing benefit eligibility through this selected funding purpose. The complete pre-vote 18 U.S.C. 611 voting rule retains its named federal-office scope. Its mixed-election exception requires all three conditions: the election is partly for another purpose; State constitutional/statutory or local-ordinance authority permits alien voting for that other purpose; and that voting is conducted independently so the alien can vote for the other purpose but has no opportunity to vote for the named federal offices. Its separate nonapplication rule also requires all three conditions: each natural parent, or each adoptive parent for an adopted alien, is or was a citizen; permanent U.S. residence before age 16; and reasonable belief in U.S. citizenship at the time of voting. No actual exception, citizenship, voting legality, violation or guilt is determined. These selected funding provisions do not rewrite those exceptions or make every act of alien voting criminal. Senate 100055 separately establishes the Bridging Immigration-related Deficits Experienced Nationwide (BIDEN) Reimbursement Fund within the Department of Justice. The Attorney General shall use the Fund amounts for grants to eligible States, State agencies, and units of local government, pursuant to their existing statutory authorities, for any of the following purposes. The paragraph 1 purpose is locating and apprehending aliens who have committed a crime under Federal, State, or local law, in addition to being unlawfully present in the United States. The paragraph 2 purpose is collection and analysis of law enforcement investigative information within the United States to counter gang or other criminal activity. The paragraph 3 purpose is investigating and prosecuting crimes committed by aliens within the United States and drug and human trafficking crimes committed within the United States. The paragraph 4 purpose is court operations related to the prosecution of crimes committed by aliens and drug and human trafficking crimes. The paragraph 5 purpose is temporary criminal detention of aliens. The paragraph 6 purpose is transporting aliens described in paragraph (1) within the United States to locations related to the apprehension, detention, and prosecution of such aliens. The paragraph 7 purpose is vehicle maintenance, logistics, transportation, and other support provided to law enforcement agencies by a State agency to enhance the ability to locate and apprehend aliens who have committed crimes under Federal, State, or local law, in addition to being unlawfully present in the United States. Paragraphs (1) and (7) retain their own additional-crime and unlawful-presence requirements; paragraph (6) retains the paragraph (1) person category, its domestic transport limit and its destination purposes. Those requirements are not imported into the other purposes. Temporary criminal detention is distinct from civil immigration detention. Court paragraph (4) prints no separate within-the-United-States phrase; no neighboring location condition is borrowed. Listed conjunctions report the source categories, not a determination that a particular grant must fund both crime categories. Existing statutory authorities do not create new State arrest/removal powers or establish actual crime/status/expense eligibility. The fund appropriation is additional fiscal year 2025 funding not to exceed $3,500,000,000 ($3.5 billion), available until September 30, 2028, for qualified and documented expenses achieving a listed purpose. The Attorney General may provide grants to State agencies and units of local government for their expenditures for completed, ongoing, or new activities determined to be eligible for such grant funding that occurred on or after January 20, 2021. That exact inclusive date is not the separate House border-reimbursement January 21 date or a new earliest date for every other appropriation. Amounts made available under this section shall be distributed to more than 1 State. This is a stated grant/distribution condition, not an actual grant, full-ceiling expenditure, complete new enforcement authority or adjudication that any recipient/expense qualifies. Other DOJ/removal and package components remain unfinished. Selected Senate 100051(9) and (10) removal purposes remain within its additional $2,055,000,000 fiscal year 2025 DHS envelope through September 30, 2029. Paragraph (9) funds expedited removal of criminal aliens in accordance with 235(b)(1); paragraph (10) funds removal of certain criminal aliens without further hearings in accordance with 235(c). Neither repeats House $75 million/$25 million earmarks, its express 212(a)(2)/(3) grounds wording or regardless-of-physical-presence phrase. The two Senate purpose labels do not themselves establish a conviction, individual inadmissibility or authority to ignore the incorporated procedures. Complete material pre-vote procedural boundaries remain bound, rather than treating these funding titles as findings of conviction or automatic removal. The captured 235(b)(1) screening rule ordinarily names arriving or designated aliens, its subparagraph (F) exception, and officer-determined 212(a)(6)(C) or (7) inadmissibility. The designated-other-alien path requires no admission or parole and failure affirmatively to show continuous physical presence for the immediately preceding two years, under the named discretionary designation authority. An asylum intention or fear of persecution triggers asylum-officer referral/interview under its own conditions. A credible-fear finding leads to detention for further asylum consideration, not an asylum grant. A negative finding retains a written record/notes and requested prompt immigration-judge review, an opportunity to be heard/questioned, the stated practicable-24-hour and hard-seven-day limits, and its own pending/final detention rules. Own pre-interview/review consultation is at no government expense and may not unreasonably delay proceedings. The defined credible-fear standard, officer training/supervision, protected-status review, administrative/collateral-review limits and complete exceptions remain, without a universal no-hearing/no-review claim or guaranteed eligibility. Captured 235(c) ordinarily names arriving-alien suspicion under 212(a)(3)(A), excluding clause (ii), or (B) or (C). Its initial officer/judge order remains subject to AG review, report and no further inquiry/hearing until directed. The AG shall review the order. The AG may order removal without further immigration-judge inquiry/hearing only if satisfied on confidential information of inadmissibility under those named grounds and, after consulting appropriate security agencies, concluding disclosure would prejudice public interest, safety or security. Both conditions are required. If that order is not made, the AG shall specify further inquiry/hearing; the alien or representative may submit a written statement and information. Suspicion is not a conviction or established inadmissibility. Complete 212(a) criminal/security grounds retain their own convictions, admissions, knowledge/reason-to-believe and other standards, exceptions and waiver references. They are not identical to felony conviction or unlawful presence. Full 212(h) and (d)(3) retain named-ground limits, complete alternatives and common conditions, excluded cases and discretionary authorities; no universal waiver or actual individual grant is inferred. Full 242(e) retains limited habeas questions and protected-status proof, District-of-Columbia system challenges with own first-implementation/appeal deadlines, remedy and inquiry limits, not ordinary inadmissibility merits review or an all-court ban. Exact January 29, 2025 Public Law 119-1 is bound with the captured 2024 provisions: its 235(b)(3) State-enforcement route and 242(f)(3) injunction exception retain their own allegations/harm/actor/scope requirements, distinct from individual review. Original 2024 bytes are not relabeled as a complete unamended 2025 Code section. No actual hearing, review, custody, waiver, crime, status or removal outcome is determined. House questions 47 and 48 are not silently settled or imported as new Senate expansion rules. The exact Senate in-accordance-with wording retains the referenced procedures; there is no new individual-removal/classification, guaranteed asylum or universal hearing/review-loss claim. Other DHS/local-support and package components remain unfinished. The selected description does not resolve legal challenges or every other package mechanism. Support/opposition applies to this complete Senate replacement. Its relationship to the earlier House choice is one underlying legislative episode; chronology alone does not establish comparability, a change of belief or a trajectory. Senate 100051(8) and (11) are purposes within the additional $2,055,000,000 fiscal year 2025 appropriation to the Secretary of Homeland Security, available through September 30, 2029. Neither purpose is a separate earmark for the full account, the ICE account or a House child appropriation. Paragraph (8) funds removal operations for specified unaccompanied alien children, but amounts under this paragraph shall only be used for permitting a specified unaccompanied alien child to withdraw the application for admission of the child pursuant to section 235(a)(4). The Secretary of Homeland Security must determine on a case-by-case basis all three specified-child conditions. First, the child has been found by an immigration officer at a land border or port of entry of the United States and is inadmissible under the Immigration and Nationality Act. Second, the child has not been a victim of severe forms of trafficking in persons, and there is no credible evidence that such child is at risk of being trafficked upon return of the child to the child's country of nationality or country of last habitual residence. Third, the child does not have a fear of returning to the child's country of nationality or country of last habitual residence owing to a credible fear of persecution. The paragraph does not print the House express contiguous-or-non-contiguous-country phrase or an independent-decision finding; neither is silently inserted into its definition. The incorporated unaccompanied-alien-child definition requires no lawful immigration status in the United States and not having attained 18 years of age, together with either no parent or legal guardian in the United States or no parent or legal guardian in the United States available to provide care and physical custody. The complete severe-forms-of-trafficking definition is bound with its own sex-trafficking and labor-or-services alternatives, force/fraud/coercion and under-18 distinctions; no label alone determines a child's eligibility. Paragraph (11) funds criminal and gang checks of defined unaccompanied alien children who are 12 years of age and older, including the examination of such unaccompanied alien children for gang-related tattoos and other gang-related markings. It prints no separate encountered-by-CBP condition; the House 70116 encounter condition is not imported. Its age-12 floor belongs to this check purpose, not the paragraph (8) withdrawal definition. Examination funding is not a finding that a child belongs to a gang, has committed a crime or is dangerous. Complete material captured pre-vote 235(a)(4) retains discretionary permission to withdraw and depart immediately, not a mandatory withdrawal or removal order. Complete TVPRA 235/1232 retains its own contiguous-child case-by-case trafficking/fear and independent-decision conditions, discretionary withdrawal/return, safe-return conditions, 48-hour screening and failed-or-undetermined-screen transfer, other-child custody pathway and own notification/72-hour-transfer exceptions. Its removal-proceedings, relief/access-to-counsel, placement, suitability and remaining safeguards retain their own scope. Senate funding does not itself establish their repeal, fulfillment or a universal individual return, protection or counsel outcome. Exact application interaction remains separate question 49; House question 43 is preserved independently. Senate 100051(5) fingerprint and DNA purposes are within the additional $2,055,000,000 fiscal year 2025 Secretary of Homeland Security account through September 30, 2029. Both purposes share the printed circumstance of aliens and alien children entering the United States without a valid visa. Subparagraph (A) funds collecting fingerprints, in accordance with section 262 and subsections (a)(3) and (b) of section 235 of the Immigration and Nationality Act. Subparagraph (B) separately funds collecting DNA, in accordance with sections 235(d) and 287(b) of that Act. These are funding purposes with their own incorporated authorities, not a determination that every alien or child is subject to every collection power or that funded collection actually occurred. Captured 262(a) concerns an alien now or hereafter in the United States who is fourteen years of age or older, has not been registered and fingerprinted under section 1201(b) or section 30 or 31 of the Alien Registration Act, 1940, and remains in the United States for thirty days or longer. All those conditions are common to its duty to apply for registration and to be fingerprinted before the expiration of such thirty days. Captured 262(b) separately requires a parent or legal guardian to apply for registration of an alien now or hereafter in the United States who is less than fourteen years of age, has not been registered under those named provisions, and remains in the United States for thirty days or longer, before that period expires. That parent/guardian provision prints registration, not the same under-14 fingerprint duty. Whenever an alien attains his fourteenth birthday in the United States, the separate rule requires in-person registration and fingerprinting within thirty days thereafter. Captured 262(c) retains the Attorney General's discretionary nonimmigrant fingerprint waiver on the basis of reciprocity pursuant to prescribed regulations; no actual waiver is inferred. Complete 235(a)(3) concerns inspection of aliens, including crewmen, who apply for or otherwise seek admission, readmission or transit; it does not itself print a fingerprint command. Complete material 235(b)(1)/(2) screening, exceptions, asylum/fear/interview/review/consultation/detention and contiguous-return conditions remain bound, together with the original favorable-admission challenge. January 29, 2025 Public Law 119-1 renumbers that original challenge from (3) to (4) and inserts the distinct State enforcement (3); the captured 2024 wording is not relabeled as an unamended 2025 subsection. Complete 235(d) retains its own belief-based conveyance search, detention/delivery with the alien-crewmember exception, named oath/evidence powers and subpoena-purpose/court-enforcement conditions. Complete 287(b) retains the designated officer/employee oath/evidence scope and its own knowing-or-willful false-evidence/perjury conditions. Neither cited provision expressly names DNA collection. That literal observation does not resolve whether other law, implementation rules or this funding language supports a proposed collection; question 50 reserves the exact DNA authority/application interaction. Question 51 separately reserves the fingerprint-purpose no-valid-visa circumstance alongside the incorporated registration age/prior-registration/duration/waiver paths and inspection procedures. No statutory repeal, guaranteed discretion outcome, universal biometric collection or actual child/parent/status/registration finding is inferred. Remaining Senate 100051 purposes (1) through (4), (6), (7) and (12) share the additional $2,055,000,000 fiscal year 2025 appropriation to the Secretary of Homeland Security, available through September 30, 2029. They are purposes within that account, not separate full-envelope earmarks or borrowed ICE/House amounts. The paragraph 1 purpose is hiring and training of additional U.S. Customs and Border Protection agents, and the necessary support staff, to carry out immigration enforcement activities. The paragraph 2 purpose is funding for transportation costs and related costs associated with the departure or removal of aliens. The paragraph 3 purpose is funding for the assignment of Department of Homeland Security employees and State officers to carry out immigration enforcement activities pursuant to sections 103(a) and 287(g) of the Immigration and Nationality Act (8 U.S.C. 1103(a) and 1357(g)). The paragraph 4 purpose is hiring additional staff and investing the necessary resources to enhance screening and vetting of all aliens seeking entry into United States, consistent with section 212 of such Act (8 U.S.C. 1182), or intending to remain in the United States, consistent with section 237 of such Act (8 U.S.C. 1227). The paragraph 6 purpose is transporting and facilitating the return, pursuant to section 235(b)(2)(C) of the Immigration and Nationality Act (8 U.S.C. 1225(b)(2)(C)), of aliens arriving from contiguous territory. The paragraph 7 purpose is funding for State and local participation in homeland security efforts for purposes of: ending the presence of criminal gangs and criminal organizations throughout the United States; addressing crime and public safety threats; combating human smuggling and trafficking networks throughout the United States; supporting immigration enforcement activities; and providing reimbursement for State and local participation in such efforts. The paragraph 12 purpose is information technology investments to support immigration purposes, including improvements to fee and revenue collections. The entry and intended-remain screening categories retain their own section 212 and section 237 references. The State/local participation list retains all five own purposes, including its own throughout-the-United-States phrases. It does not borrow the reimbursement fund's crime-plus-unlawful-presence category or domestic transport restriction. The general departure/removal transportation purpose prints no separate within-the-United-States phrase. The assignment list retains Department of Homeland Security employees and State officers pursuant to both printed statutory references, not authority for any State employee to exercise all Federal powers. The printed purpose lists do not determine that a particular expenditure must fulfill every listed category. Fee and revenue collection IT is not a new fee, fine or penalty charge. Complete captured 103(a) retains its named agency roles, regulatory/delegation powers, consents and other conditions. In captured 103(a)(10), the Attorney General may authorize a State or local law enforcement officer to perform or exercise any of the powers, privileges, or duties conferred or imposed by this chapter or regulations issued thereunder upon officers or employees of the Service only in the event of the Attorney General's determination that an actual or imminent mass influx of aliens arriving off the coast of the United States, or near a land border, presents urgent circumstances requiring an immediate Federal response, and with the consent of the head of the department, agency, or establishment under whose jurisdiction the individual is serving. The captured event-specific authorization does not establish general unconditioned State power. Previously bound full 287(g) agreement qualifications, training, written powers/duration, Federal direction/supervision, voluntary/communication/cooperation and expense/employment/liability distinctions remain unchanged. Complete captured section 212(a) grounds and remaining operative section 212 authorities retain their own standards, exceptions, discretionary waivers and conditional notice rules, not an every-alien crime finding or guaranteed notice/waiver. January 29, 2025 Public Law 119-1 replaces the original Attorney General references in 212(d)(5) with Secretary of Homeland Security and adds the distinct State enforcement route. Original captured 2024 words are preserved with that amending law, not relabeled as the complete unamended 2025 section. Complete captured section 237 retains distinct deportability grounds, actual conviction/knowledge/timing or other own requirements, exceptions/waivers, special nonimmigrant and SIJ boundaries and conditional administrative stays; screening funding does not determine an individual inadmissible, deportable or criminal. The contiguous-return purpose is pursuant to 235(b)(2)(C). The captured 235(b)(2)(C) return authority concerns an applicant for admission whom the examining immigration officer determines is not clearly and beyond a doubt entitled to be admitted, arriving on land (whether or not at a designated port of arrival) from a foreign territory contiguous to the United States. The Attorney General may return that alien to that territory pending a proceeding under section 1229a. The captured parent exceptions for a crewman, an alien to whom paragraph (1) applies, and a stowaway remain. Discretionary return is not a final removal order or universal cross-border return duty. Complete captured 240 proceedings retain judge/charge/exclusive-procedure exceptions, own representation and evidence/examination limits, burdens, decision/appeal, motion and notice/deadline/stay rules. No guaranteed relief, government-paid counsel or individual hearing/return result is inferred. Other H.R.1 immigration components and separately reserved application questions remain unfinished. The Senate 90005(b) State Border Security Reinforcement Fund is a distinct DHS fund. Its complete selected operative clauses are retained below. Senate 90005(b) paragraph 1: There is established, in the Department of Homeland Security, a fund to be known as the ``State Border Security Reinforcement Fund.'' Senate 90005(b) paragraph 2: The Secretary of Homeland Security shall use amounts appropriated or otherwise made available for the Fund for grants to eligible States and units of local government for any of the following purposes: Senate 90005(b) purpose A: Construction or installation of a border wall, border fencing or other barrier, or buoys along the southern border of the United States, which may include planning, procurement of materials, and personnel costs related to such construction or installation. Senate 90005(b) purpose B: Any work necessary to prepare the ground at or near land borders to allow construction and maintenance of a border wall or other barrier fencing. Senate 90005(b) purpose C: Detection and interdiction of illicit substances and aliens who have unlawfully entered the United States and have committed a crime under Federal, State, or local law, and transfer or referral of such aliens to the Department of Homeland Security as provided by law. Senate 90005(b) purpose D: Relocation of aliens who are unlawfully present in the United States from small population centers to other domestic locations. Senate 90005(b) paragraph 3: In addition to amounts otherwise available for the purposes described in paragraph (2), there is appropriated for fiscal year 2025, out of any money in the Treasury not otherwise appropriated, to the Department of Homeland Security for the State Border Security Reinforcement Fund established by paragraph (1), $10,000,000,000, to remain available until September 30, 2034, for qualified expenses for such purposes. Senate 90005(b) paragraph 4: The Secretary of Homeland Security may provide grants from the fund established by paragraph (1) to State agencies and units of local governments for expenditures made for completed, ongoing, or new activities, in accordance with law, that occurred on or after January 20, 2021. Senate 90005(b) paragraph 5: Each State desiring to apply for a grant under this subsection shall submit an application to the Secretary containing such information in support of the application as the Secretary may require. The Secretary shall require that each State include in its application the purposes for which the State seeks the funds and a description of how the State plans to allocate the funds. The Secretary shall begin to accept applications not later than 90 days after the date of the enactment of this Act. Senate 90005(b) paragraph 6: Nothing in this subsection shall authorize any State or local government to exercise immigration or border security authorities reserved exclusively to the Federal Government under the Immigration and Nationality Act (8 U.S.C. 1101 et seq.) or the Homeland Security Act of 2002 (6 U.S.C. 101 et seq.). The Federal Emergency Management Agency may use not more than 1 percent of the funds made available under this subsection for the purpose of administering grants provided for in this section. The paragraph (2)(C) alien category retains both unlawful entry and commission of a crime under Federal, State, or local law; those alien predicates do not classify illicit substances. Transfer or referral remains as provided by law. Paragraph (2)(D) instead concerns unlawful presence and relocation from small population centers to other domestic locations; it does not borrow the crime or unlawful-entry predicates from (C), or authorize an international return. Only (A) specifies the southern border; (B) says at or near land borders. The paragraph (2) eligible-State/local-unit grant purpose rule and paragraph (4) discretionary State-agency/local-government expenditure rule remain distinct. The paragraph (5) application obligations name each State; no additional local-government obligation is inferred. The 90-day clause concerns when the Secretary must begin accepting applications, not an applicant deadline or a finding that applications are open. The paragraph (6) construction rule preserves exclusively Federal authorities without deciding which actual functions or expenditures fall within that reservation. The FEMA administration ceiling is discretionary, no more than 1 percent of funds under this subsection for grants in this section; its two scope words remain distinct. This is not an actual award, expenditure, eligibility, individual status/crime, relocation, power delegation or reimbursement determination. House reimbursement amounts, availability, January 21 date and duplicate-reimbursement restriction are not imported. Other package components and the 51 separately reserved application questions remain unfinished. Selected Senate 90005(a) funding and its own program context follow. Senate 90005(a) paragraph 1: In addition to amounts otherwise available, there is appropriated to the Administrator of the Federal Emergency Management Agency for fiscal year 2025, out of any money in the Treasury not otherwise appropriated, to remain available until September 30, 2029, to be administered under the State Homeland Security Grant Program authorized under section 2004 of the Homeland Security Act of 2002 (6 U.S.C. 605), to enhance State, local, and Tribal security through grants, contracts, cooperative agreements, and other activities-- Senate 90005(a) purpose A: $500,000,000 for State and local capabilities to detect, identify, track, or monitor threats from unmanned aircraft systems (as such term is defined in section 44801 of title 49, United States Code), consistent with titles 18 and 49 of the United States Code; Senate 90005(a) purpose B: $625,000,000 for security and other costs related to the 2026 FIFA World Cup; Senate 90005(a) purpose C: $1,000,000,000 for security, planning, and other costs related to the 2028 Olympics; and Senate 90005(a) purpose D: $450,000,000 for the Operation Stonegarden Grant Program. Senate 90005(a) paragraph 2: None of the funds made available under subparagraph (B) or (C) of paragraph (1) shall be subject to the requirements of section 2004(e)(1) or section 2008(a)(12) of the Homeland Security Act of 2002 (6 U.S.C. 605(e)(1), 609(a)(12)). The pre-vote fiscal year 2024 DHS/FEMA HSGP notice reproduced on Hawaii's official host describes Operation Stonegarden as supporting enhanced cooperation and coordination among CBP, USBP, and Federal, State, local, Tribal and territorial law enforcement agencies to improve overall border security. It funds joint border-security efforts along routes of ingress and egress to and from international borders, including travel corridors in States bordering Mexico and Canada and States and territories with international water borders. In that notice, those State, local, Tribal and territorial law enforcement agencies use their inherent law enforcement authorities and receive no additional authority from participating in Stonegarden. This is dated program-purpose context, not a new power conferred by the Senate appropriation or a complete 2025 eligibility rule. The additional fiscal year 2025 appropriation names FEMA Administrator, availability until September 30, 2029, administration under the State Homeland Security Grant Program in 6 U.S.C. 605, and State/local/Tribal security through grants, contracts, cooperative agreements and other activities. The Stonegarden purpose is $450,000,000 within that administration provision. The drone-threat, FIFA and Olympics purposes retain their own printed objects and amounts as adjacent context; those purposes alone do not establish an immigration purpose. The exemption from 605(e)(1) minimum allocation and 609(a)(12) grant-administration expense cap expressly names only FIFA paragraph (1)(B) and Olympics paragraph (1)(C); no exemption for Stonegarden paragraph (1)(D) or drone paragraph (1)(A) is inferred. Captured 605(e)(1) retains its State and named-territory minimum-allocation branches, own fiscal-year denominators and percentages; captured 609(a)(12) permits expenses directly related to grant administration except that such expenses may not exceed 3 percent of the grant amount. Neither this cap nor those minima are reclassified as the separate 90005(b) FEMA one-percent ceiling. Complete captured 603, 605 and 609 retain their own program relationships, application/distribution/multistate rules, permitted-use and personnel/construction/recreation restrictions, waivers, reimbursement, transfers and equipment requirements. Their application to a particular 2025 Stonegarden award, including interaction with the dated 2024 notice's separate HSGP components and conditions, is reserved as question 52. No 2024 funding amount, application deadline, performance period, subrecipient tier or approval automatically governs this new appropriation. No particular State/local/Tribal award, entitlement, expenditure, additional law-enforcement power or individual status result is inferred.
